THE DIGNITY OF LABOUR. Industrious hands, their labours plying, Work on in friendly league, and so, Each in his craft with other vying, Mr Their powers to higher achievement grow. To guard fair freedom's sacred treasure, Master and man their force unite, Each in his station finds his pleasure, And pays the scorner slight for slight. ' Toil is the burgher's crown of merit, His guerdon some true blessing won: Kings from the state which they inherit. Take honour, ire from the things we've done. —From "The Song of the Bell," translated by Sir Theo- dore Martin, in Mackwood's Magazine for April.

THREE LITTLE RATS. Three little rats took off their data, And sat them down to read; Three bigger rats came and stole those hats— r A very great shame indeed! Oh, no one knew, and yet 'tis true, About those rats' three hats; You poor little rats, with no nice hats! Full soon you'll know your need. • Soon these little rats looked round for their hats]: (They'd read their papers through), Then these little rats, they missed their hats— They were just as good as new— " Oh, dear !" they cried, standing side by side, "Will nobody find our hats 2" • Oh, poor little rats, without your hats, • The loss you'll surely rue. ' Well, these little rats, without their hats, • '• Had toothache very sore! And as these rats ne'er found their hats, They had to buy some more. But from that day, so I've heard say, They ne'er took off their hats; And those little rats never lost their hats, As they had once before. —Little Folks', Magazine for April.

div.p: Tarittitg.

_ "Why do summer roses fade?" is a question asked by the poet. "Because there is no way of re-leaving them, the answer of the gardener. A seaman who had escaped from shipwreck was asked lac a lady how he felt when the waves broke over him. *Vet, ma'am," he said; "very wet." "If you call this skinning," said Tom to the barber, "it's not so bad; but if you call it shaving I should prefer your using the other side of the razor." Re ran somewhat hastily into a cigar shop, and said pompously, "Give me one of your best Matilda cigars." "I suppose j7ou mean Manilla?" said the assistant. "Oh, yes," he answered; "I was thinking of another girl." " Come in, my poor man," said a benevolent lady to a weed tramp, "and.! will get you something to eat." Thanky, mum; don't care if I do." "I suppose," con- tinued the lady, setting a square meal before him, "your life has been full of trials?" "Yes, mum are the wust slit wuz I allus got convicted." Clara—" They say Charley is a great catch, and all the girls are running after him; but for my part I don't see what they find in him to admire." Sarah—" Perhaps you do not know that his mother has the reputation of being a wretched cook." Clara—"ls that so? 'dell make a splendid husband for somebody." Two old men lamenting the changes that have taken place. First old man (sadly)—" I cannot enjoy myself sow as-I could when I was a boy. I can't eat half as much." Second old man—" I cannot eat as much now as I could when I was a boy, but I regard that as rather a wise provision." "Why so?" "Because I haven't half as much to eat." The town of Pequog„ Massachussetts, puts in its claim for the champion snorer: The young wife of an elderly sesident. awakening from a sound sleep, began to shake her slumbering lord smartly to make him stop snoring. Just then there came several very loud rolls of thunder, and, desisting from her attempt, she resigned herself quietly to sleep, remarking, "It is only4hunderlng, after • ail; I thought you were snoring." . Too Loptc.m.—Sometimes strange difficulties are en- eountered by the young ladies who are endeavouring to teach Christianity to the Chinese in the Sunday schools of the metropolis. One of the most conscientious, as well as *vie of the brightest and prettiest of these teachers was attempting in a Brooklyn school recently to inculcate upon the heathen mind of a sleek-looking Mongolian the lessen of charity towards all "God loves everyone," she said. "We should love everyone." The Chinaman • looked meekly up into her face and quietly asked, "Does God love me?" "Yes," the young lady replied. "Do you love everyone?" was the next pointed inquiry. "yea," she answered. "Do you love me ?" " Y-y-yes." "Will you marry me ?" There was no direct answer to this question, but the teacher has since changed her pupil for a Chinaman of less logical turn of mind. YORKSHIIIE Fotx.—ln the April number of the Quiver the Bishop of Ripon draws attention to "The Work of the Church in Yorkshire." In the course of his paper his lordship refers to the musical tastes of the West Riding men, remarking' "Music, it has been thought, cleaves to the hills and shuns the plains, and a chorus- leader who had much knowledge of musical taste in Yorkshire said, that to the east of the little brook which separated the East from the West Riding there was com- paratively little music, while to the west it flourished and V 7354 loved. Afilance at the map will show that the _ _ _

East Riding is usually flat, and the West Riding abounds in hills. It is certainly true that when we climb we are • tempted to sing, as we seldom are when we tread a level road; aspiration and the sense of upward progress find • utterance in song. But, whatever the explanation may be, music prevails in the West Riding of Yorkshire, and is tittle else than a passion amongst the people. This love 43f music is not, however, accompanied by any mere feeble sentimentalism of character. On the contrary, it is, as every one knows, allied with a shrewd, strong, and independent character. This shrewdness and independ- ence shows itself in many ways, and breaks out, perhaps in its most striking form, in the quaint sayings and quick answers of which so many stories are told. As an example, take the following :—A. curate and his wife who had worked in a Yorkshire village received some appointment in the south of England. The curate's -wife, who had tlot shown much tact, went about the village tellin with somewhat ostentatious pleasure the news that 1-hey were about to leave, and dilating with more fume as than wisdozr upon the elite character of the People . the future sphere of their work. She was indulsir .g herself in this vein in one of the cottages, and the good woman that the parish to which umsy, • were going, was full of gentlefolk. "Nobody," she 84Lcs "in the whole parish is otherwise than well-to-do— y are all ladies and gentlemen." The Yorkshire IV omen, without looking up from her ironing, quietly remarked," I reckon that there will be an alteration when you get there." Another side of their character is illus- trated by the following southern clergyman wont some years ago to preach in a district church in a York- shire town. When his sermon was over and he entered the vestry, the churchwarden expressed his satisfaction with the clergyman's efforts in the pulpit by saying, "You have done yourself good in coming." Tint bite OF PATMOS.—Of course the stock sight of Patmos is the cave in which tradition says St. John wrote down his Revelations. There are many caves in the island, and, for my part, I 'feel sceptical as to this one being what it professes; for lit must have been ex- ceedingly shallow before the church was built on to it, and moreover, too much exposed to view for secret meditation, seeing that it is commanded by the site of the old town a little way up the opposite hill on the road to the monastery.T.At present, however, the cave is sufficiently concealed from view by a pile of buildings fast falling into'ruins; where a few years ago existed a school for the education of Greeks: but now that local education is much improved in the Levent, parents do not care to send their sons so far, and the school has been closed. The care of the churches one adjoining and one over the cave—is entrusted to a priest—Papa Makarios by name—and his sister Sophia, who occupy rooms in the ramshackle building. On the first occasion on which we visited the cave, we were lucky in finding Sophia alone, for she is deeply imbued with the legends of the place, and the story of Kynops is as much a part of her creed as the existence of St. John is of ours. She is a garrulous, energetic old dame; and, in the absence of her brother, volunteered to show us the cave and the church of St. Anna, which was built up to it by St. Christodoulos. She was almost theatrical in her gestures, as she showed us the points of interest therein. Here was the bole in the rock in which St. John nlaced his pillow when he slept; by- the side of it was tbelhole, bv the aid of which St. John raised himself from the ground when he got up.. Over these holes a rude cross was shown us, which, Sophia said, the saint had wrought with his own hands. Then she showed us two holes in the roof, to which St. John was in the habit of tYhiff himself by a cord, so that he might not fall asleep when he said his prayers. But the greatest object ef Sophia's veneration, before which she crossed herself and knelt, was a triple rent in the rock, from which she affirmed that the voice of the Holy Trinity had issued with the divine message to the theologian. Every crack and fissure in the rock is aseociated with something sacred, and as a rememberance of the place, Sophia pre- sented us with some chips of the rock; and it m occurredust to us that if she did the same to every 174,6112, she have considerably altered the dimensions of the cave. We bought a pretty little carved wooden bowl, in which the priest kept his incense for burning in the church Sophia eats to andhe r a rPaati, aaye, and then were conducted by Sop merit, where she regaled us with sweet as she related to us wonderful stories concerning the religious ecstasies into which worshippers et the shrine edvaeyuosf at hgreeat ht od elsco giiiapn- tin w:reowf wont thfesTiov.alMhelterd wahererdg gave hthe —how they hold real vigil in the church during the whole of the night before, and how the monks come down from the monastery with their relics and their banners in grand procession, to worship in the cave.—Blackwood's ifagazine for irarch.

One rough March day the Chief Justice was alighting from his carriage at the entrance to the Four Courts, Dublin, as his official came puffing and blowing from the effects of the gale. "You seem quite out of breath," said the Chief Justice, as he shook hands with his official. "Yes," replied the other, "as I came along the quays the wind was cutting my face." "Upon my wc.:rd," gravely replied the Chief Justice, "I think the wind had the worst of it."

Cam:oar/Vs Pocasrr MONRY.—Teach children the proper use of money. Begin with a small allowance of pocket money which they shall feel is their ownsand let an account of its expenditure be made to you. Carefully. guard against any ridicule if there have been any fqolish purchases, for that will soon beget distrust, then follows deceit, and very soon you will never know what has become of the money. Kindly advise, so that if your boy is tempted to spend his money in a way he knows is wrong he will freely come to you and tell of it. Until you feel positively compell4l to do it do not withdraw your allowance. It may be that you'avill flnd'Oo other way to stop a career of wasteful and sinful extravagance. But let all effort be made in other ways first. Teach your boys to earn a little for themselves. Many little ways will suggest themselves. It is so much more help- ful to them, as well as an enjoyable pride, that it is always well to encourage an such endeavour. We know a mother who prizes, above all her other possessions, a a pair of gold sleeve buttons purchased with the first money her boy ever earned, and though he is now in business for himself, we fancy that he never invested any money more cheerfully than that. 6LADSTONE. —Mrs. Gladstone's share in her husband's labours and triumphs, no less than in his recreations and his defeats, has been constant, yet she has not allowed it to extinguish what we may term her own individuality—the natural bent and tendencies of her generous, womanly' sympathies. There can be no doubt that it is as the prime mover in several important philanthropic agencies that her name will be best remem- bered by posterity. It Was in the year 1866 that one of the cholera epidemics which have often caused such ravages on the Continent of Europe threatened our own shores. It did more; it visited us, with comparative mildness truly, but with sufficient severity to stir to ' their depths the charitable instincts and philanthropi6 energies of the British public. However we may dispute and speculatq over the "place" of woman in creation and in practical life, no one questions the propriety of her interference by the sick-beds of the poor In the hot- pital or at their own homes. Mrs. Gladstone was one of the first to set the example Of organised sympathy and well-directed aid; and the relief that was afforded by the higher classes of English people to the poorer sufferers by this dire epidemic, was due in no small degree to her personal influence. She constantly visited the hospital wards in London and sent a band of the "sisters" who were connected with the well-known church of All Saints, Margaret-street, to minister to the sufferings and relieve the wants of the sick and dying poor. This was, in fact, the prelude to her undertaking the labours with which her name will be more especially identified, vit, the establishment of Convalescent Homes. —The Lady's World.

COMPARATIVE PRICES OF BREAD AND MEAT /N RECENT YEARS—During the eight years which preceded the abolition in 180, the total duties levied on corn, meal, and flour only averaged £707,651 per annum. From 1850 to 1869, the registration fee of one shilling, charged on each quarter imnorted, yielded on the average an annual revenue of £623,000. In 1869, in order, as tho Chancellor of the Exchequer remarked, "to do away with the last rag of protection," this fee was repealed. Had it been retained, we 'should, on the 230 millions of quarters imported between 1870 and 1885, have saved 11+ millions sterling of revenue, .or over £700,000 a year. We say saved, for as we shall later on show, these millions wholly went to swell the profits of the foreign importer. Between 1840 and 1849, we imported of corn, meal, and flour in all 41 mil- lipns of quarters, from which we derived a gross revenue of £6,817,848, about 3s. 4d. per quarter. The repeal seems to have had no effect on market value, for though it ruled low in 1851 and 1852, that could not, as we im- ported 7,000 quarters of wheat less in those years than we did in 1849 and 1850, have been caused by supplies from abroad. The market prices of wheat, as given in 1 "the abstracts," and the contract prices of the 4-lb. loaf, supplied to the Seamen's Hospital at Greenwich, averaged' as follows : 1

The prices of the loaf here quoted being by contract for large quantities, private consumers would doubtless have to pay more. We shallassume, therefore, that from 1841-50, when the baker was content with less exor- bitant profits, the retail price of the loaf averaged 70. To-day it is ed. If we allow two 41b. loaves ,a week as the consumption of a working man, we get 13s. 3d. he per annum pays less now for his bread than he did from 1841-50. But what is he paying for his meat? It is difficult to get at the prices now paid for meat by a working man, but from all we can learn, we believe it is on the average not under 7d. per pound. If we allow him half a pound per day, this comes to £5 Bs. in the year; while if we take it he did not pay more than 4d. per pound in 1850, the difference shows he pays to-day 465. more for his meat, and 13s. 3d. less for his bread, or net 325. 9d., that he annually now pays more on these two items, without taking into account the higher rates he pays for butter a id eggs.—From "Free Trade and Depressed Trade," by A. Wilhansson, in • "Blackwood's Magazine" for April, 1887. _

BISHOP Fassra's Lovs ov SPOUT.—Bishop Fraser was not a muscular Christian: in some respects his mind was very different indeed from the character of that brotherhood' and perhaps it is only the mild flavour of the subdued Berserker in the biographer which makes us think of those innocent giants of the past. To be himself so mild a man, no one could be more dis- tinctively muscular than the author of "Tom Brown"; and there is something in the fondness with which he lingers upon certain characteristics of his present hero, which recalls to us the more congenial souls upon whom he could have expatiated with so much more hearty enthusiasm. If not muscular, however, Bishop Fraser was distinctly manly—not more so in the frank and robust character of his mind than in the delight he took in walking, driving, riding, and, above all, in horses—a taste which commends him greatly to his historian, as it did to his pupils in earlier years, and as we don't doubt it will do to the majority of English readers. We are doubtful, for our own part, how far the love of horses really is an elevating and wholesome passion; It has results upon certain minds which are not perhaps en tirely satisfactory. But there is no taste which meets.with so much response, in England at least, or is accepted as so entirely a part of a loveable Sand generous character. We cannot help feeling that it is above all others the thing which attracts Mr. Hughes to the late Bishop of Manchester. There are many other points of interest in the Bishop's character, and he is one of those examples of spotless and upright manhood which Mr. Hughes has done so much to make the ideal of English youth; but it is this passion—this weakness. shallwe call it ?—this predilection, which endears the subject of the , memoir to the writer of it; and thus throws a humorous half pathetic reflection upon the time when every zealous priest of his tribe was likewise a fine cricketer, a handy oar, a strong swimmer, a gallant horseman—keeping his muscles well abreast of his religion, and counting handi- ness and hardiness next to godliness. There were giants in those days. Perhaps our young clergy have not actually fallen off in muscular development, or resigned the priae of thews and sinews for other accompaniments of spiritual life; but the day of Kingsley and his stalwart race is over. The fashion of one generation is not that of another. Lawn-tennis, with its possibilities of femi- nine intervention, does not perhaps string the nerves as did the more strenuous struggleS of an elder day.—From "The Old Saloon," ha Blackwood, Magazine for April, 1887.

country—to be kind and indulgent to the minority that had kept away from -their ..ranks. That had gone on "to a certain eXtent, hut it could not be allowed to go on when the Liberal Unionists allied themselves with Tory management to the extent they were now doing. It was time that they dis- tinctly Feld 4‘Vidatfar you have 'gone ;'btit notur- thei. ft you go .on with the Coercion Bill, you leave us. We will be no party to this any longer." During the five years Mr. McMinniei was the)r re- presentative, a Coercion Bill was running to its full length. That waitt terminable bill, but the one now proposed was for all time. A special meeting of the General Council of. this Association was held on Saturday eveniag, the object for which it was called being to consulter: a resolution, of which notice had been given; Protest- ing against the Coercion Bill introduced into. the House of Commons by the present Government. There was a good attendance of members. Mr. J. G. McMinnies, president of the Association, occupied the chair, and amongst those also present were the Revs. R. Pilcher, 8.A., E. Moore, and G. E. Cutting; Alderman Burgess; Councillors F. A. Roberts, W. Pierpoint, H. Fleming. and H. Roberts (secretary of 1 the Association); Dr. i Gornall ; Messrs C. S. Bur- gess, E. J. Guest, S. Barlow, H. Whitham, T' Bir- chen, S. Kenyon. L. Sutcliffe, Bromley, &c. • • The SECRETARY (Mr. H. Roberts) read 'a notice received from the National Liberal Federation, and it was resolved that Alderman Burgess, Councillor W. Pierpoint, and Councillor F. A. Roberts be appointed a deputation to 'represent the Association at the meeting of the Federation to be held in London on the following Wednesday; to ccrnsfderthe Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill. , The SztnirrAriv then read the following letter received from the Rev. John Yonge :—" I regret that I am unable to attend the meeting convened for this evening to denounce the Bill devited by the Government to rivet the fetters of a cruel and un- just bondage upon the Irish people. I hope that no , faltering or uncertain sound will go forth from to- night's meeting upon this matter, but that it will be made abundantly clear that the overwhelming majority of Warrington Liberals, as epresented in the meeting, is in deadly opposition to this last and worst measure of coercion. It is, the. 'worst' simplyhecause, bad as all such other bills have been, this immeasurably surpasses them all., And it is the ' last ' because never again, as I firmly believe, will a policy of coercion for Ireland be propounded in the British Parliament. This is a time for clear, definite, and emphatic speech upon the part of all true Liberals, and all true lovers of justice and equity, freedom, and friendship be- tween Great Britain and Ireland. In my opinien, men who vote for this .. bill can ••• no longer claim' to be 'called true Liberals. It is with greater regret than I can describe', that I see many who have been foremost in our party; both locally and nationally','-now rallying to the support of a measure like this. I -cannot forget their past invaluable services, but it is hard to com- prehend' or forgive them for their action now. Time will show, as I believe, that we are the Unionists, and they the Separatists. I hope your meeting to-night is but the prelude to a larger meeting in the Public Hall." (Cheers.) The Cumulus:, who was, remeived with cheers, said that they had met to consider, and, he hoped, to condemn, the Bill which the Gqvernment bad introduced into the House of Commons, and which they called the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) 'Bill. Other people called it the eighty-eighth Coer- cion. Bill of this century. The measure was one so important that4ie should like to say a few words upon it. In'the first place, in his opinion, the bill was entirely unnecessary. (Cheers.) No case had been made out for it. On the contrary, the attempt to make out a case had signally failed. In. 1885 all parties, including the Tories themselves, had come to the conclusion that further coercion was unneces- sary and futile. A change had now come over the opinions of the Tory party, and they had introduced this new Coercion Bill. It had been shown in the House of Commons that of serious offences in 1885 there were 512. In 1886 there were 518, so that the difference in criminal offences between 1885, when everyone said coercion was unnecessary, and 1886, amounted to six. What they had found in reference to coercion was that all Coercion Acts had been en- tirelyfutile. and he had no doubt that this last Coercion Bill would be entirely futile' also. It was an Act which contained provisions entirely repug- nant to the opinions of every true and generous- minded Liberal. (Cheers.)- They would observe that eertain crimes were withdrawn entirely from the jurisdietion of judges and juries, and those crimes were to be dealt with by resident magistrates in Ireland. What those resident magistrates in Ire- land were Mr. Morley.had told. Mr. Morley said of a resident magistrate that he was not in the least degree accustomed to weigh evidence, he had had in nine cases out of ten no legal training what- ever, and was a creature of the Central authority, the Castle, as it was called, in Dublin. To.puch gentlemen was to be given the trial of prisoners in- dicted for certain crimes, in the absence of both judge and jury. Another and a more outrageous proposal in the bill was that Irish prisoners should be brought over to London to be tried there. His own opinion Was that nothing so infamous, so out- rageous. so unjust, was ever proposed. in their time at least, to the House of Commons. (Cheers). They had beentold during the last day or two that this most , infamous proposal had been withdrawn, or would be withdrawn, by the Government, and that with- drawal Was said to be at the instigation of that party in the House calling themselves Liberal Unionists. That might be so, but he must say that the last speech made by Lord Hartington did not seem to him to give any countenance to that report, or to suggest that the Unionists, as they called themselves, were pressing Government to withdraw that clause. There was-just one paint he wished to remark upon. They would observe that this bill, if it was carried out, would be carried by the assis- tance of so-called Liberals. ("Shame.") He could not express to them the regret he felt to see men. like Lord Hartington. Mr. Chamberlain, Sir Henry James, and others, joining with the Tory party in carrying such a tyrannous measure.. They (the Liberals) had spoken very kindly about friends who had left them. They had seen one after another of them returned to Parliament who had submitted themselves to the unspeakable humilia- tion of being returned by the aid of Tory votes, and they had been silent; they had heard these gentle- men say in the House of Commons that they were sitting there, and would continue to sit there, to maintain a Tory Government in power,and to keep a Liberal Government out, and they had said nothing. The time was come when they must speak. (Cheers.) They had "gone out from us," and their actions since had proved " they were not of us." He was very glad to see such a large number. of people present to protest against a measure which was an injustice and an insult to Ireland, and which, if passed, would deteriorate the charac- ter of the British House of Commons in the eyes of the world. (Cheers.) Councillor W. PIERPO/NT said that the remarks of the chairman must have gone deep in the minds of every Liberal present, and of some of their Unionist friends. Ireland had had 86 or 87 coer- cion bills, and this last was to be imposed upon, her entirely through the fact that the Liberals were supporting the Tory Government in a policy that was a disgrace to the times in which we lived. A resolution he had to propose expressed pretty muth what he thought on this subject. It was as fol- lows :—"That this meeting, being of opinion that the Government has shown no reasonable grounds for the application of further repressive legislation ito the Irish people, and believing also that the true remedy for Irish discontent cannot be found in coercion, but rather in a wise and just extension of the power of self-government, such as has been propounded by Mr. Gladstone. emphatically de- nounces the new Coercion Bill as an unjustifiable and base attempt to rivet the fetters of a cruel arid unjust bondage upon our fellow-countrymen, and pledges itself to use all possible means to prevent such an infamous measure passing into law, He did believe that there was no reasonable ground ter the Bill, and he said that the Liberal party, if they believed in such a miserable policy, should be ashamed of themselves. The argement's of Liberal Unionists were of no use. He wanted an argument of Christianity, and not one of force. He wanted one of doing,as he would be done by. There was nothing in a Coercion Bill that resembled doing that towards Ireland which we should like Ireland to do towards us. (Cheers.) What would be said to a Dublin Castle in England? (A Voice': "Pull it down.") Yes, and they wouldremove the men who upheld it. (Cheese.) He agreed with the chair- man that now was the time to speak out. They . had been led too long by aristocratic Whigs. If Mr. Chamberlain wanted to creep up the sleeve ot the aristocracy, let him do it, but he must have no support from the Liberal party. .Ireland had been discontented since the Union, a union founded upon fraud, and maintained by fraud. A discontented Ire- lant meant no good to England, but a great annual expense, and with a contented Ireland there would be a more peaceful and better England, more con- tent among the labouring populaticn, better trade, and more money, stirring all round. He had great pleasure in proposing the resolution. (Cheers.) Mr. F. A. ROBERTS • seconded the resolution. He of the resolution had said, and be also thought that thoroughly agreed, he said, with what the proposer it was time, as the chairman said, that they as Liberals should bestir themselves and speak out with no uncertain voice. They had done their best —in warrington as well as in other parts of the,

The Rev. R. PILCHER heartily concurred with the resolu- tion. Re did not believe in saying strong things about the, Unionists ;they had got plenty of brains and, he believed, a grist deal of boneetv. At the sam, time, he was convinced that they had come to the parting of the ways. A Um and temperate enunciation of their principles would be quits sufficient to enable them to be the survival of the fittest. (Cheers.)

, Mr. H. Warrifeaf was also convinced that they had come to the parting at the ways. If the Liberal Unionists were prepared to go down one track, be asa Liberal was prepared te follow another. He protested against the measure. (Cheers.)—
Mr. S., BARLOW said he believed that Mr. Parnell had tern the Coercion Bill into raga, and he did not thick it Would pass in the state% which it would be introduced to the Honse. (Cheers.),
BROMI:ZY alsrispoke briefly In favour of the resolu- tion.

, Mr. H. Roawns said that he had felt for a long time that it was a difficult matter to speak with reserve and modera- tion of the conduct of the Liberal Unionists. He respected the ability of Mr. Chamberlain, if only for his Bankruptcy legislation, but his respect could not blind him to the fact that Mr. Chamberlain's conduct now was unworthy of a Liberal and of a man who aspired to lead the Radical party in the House of Commons. If the Unionists would only be honest, and if the English people could have the ease pat before them apart from preinclia*, religious bigotry, and intolerance, he was sure that it would not be long before it would be possikle to pass Mr. Gladstone's bill. ICheers.) The resolution was then carried unanimously, and It WIl& further resolved that a petition, based on the terms of the resolution, be signed by the chairman and forwarded to the House of Commons.

The passing of a veto of thanks to the chairman brought' the proceedings to a close. REPLIES TO THE RESOLUTION. In accordance with the resolutions passed at last Satur- day night's meeting of the Warrington Liberal Council, copies of the resolution were forwarded, to several of the principal members of Parliament. Among those who have acknowledged its receipt are Mr. Gladstone, Lord Granville, tlle William Harcourt, Mr. John Morley, Dr. Lyon 141avfair. The Right Hon. the Marquis ofßi pon replied as follows STVD&BY ROYAL, 'brow, 6th „ Dear sir,--r have received your letter of the 4th met, forwarding me a copy of a resolution passed unanimously at a meeting of the G.neral Council of the Warrington Liberal Association. I have read that resolution wilds great satisfaction, and rejoice to find that the Liberals of War- rington condemn, without hesitation, the new ,Uotareion Bill for Ireland which has been proposed by the Government, and cilculated, it seems to me, ta inflict grievous injustice upon Ireland and serious disgrace upon the zillion at large. —I am, sir, yours truly, RIPON." The Hight Hon. Earl Spencer writes:— " ALTHORP, NORT:AIAIIPT3N, 7th•Anitts4 1887. Sir,—l have received the copy of a resolution passed at a meeting of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Association. I entirely agree. with the petition taken up in the House of Commons by Mr. Gladstone with regard to the Irish policy of the Government. I am, satisfied that the enforcement of exceptional, legislation in Ireland will °sly Increase the difficulties cf governing that country on the present system, and I agree with the resolution that the trail. remedy for Irish discortent is to bo fonnd in a wise and just extension of the power of soffsgovernment.—Yonrs, faithfully, SPENCE.D." The Right Ron. B.C. E. Childers wrote : • 'e, ay. GHORIWS. PLACE, EIXOE PA3IIC CORNEA, sth April 1887. Sir,-4 am in roceipt of your letter Of the 4th inst., en- closing the copy of a resolution adopted bv &General Coun- cil of the Warrington Liberal Association, in condemnation of the Irish Coercion Bill. I hope that this Bill, which. if carried, will ha my judgment indict great evils both on Ire- land and Great Britain, may receive the strenuous opposition of all earnest Liberals. The choice, apparently, now Bea between a measure granting to Irish- men the management of theV own inttrnal affairs, and a measure depriving Irishmed of their principal liber- ties, especially trial by jury in Ireland, and this not for a time but permanently. In face of sntb an issue, I hope that all minor differences will be for a time forgotten, and that Liberals will close their ranks..—l have the honour to be, air vour obedient servant, HMI C. E. CnitnEns.'

JUBILEE.

On Monday: 'evening a meeting of the General I Jubilee Committee was beltlin the Council Chamber, I Town Hell, for the purpose of appoieting an execu- tive committee. The Mayor (Alderman Picltmere) I presided, and there was a large attendance, Which included delegates from the Friendly, Trade, and other societies and Sunday schools.

The MAvon suggested that it would, perhaps, be best to first cnnsider the question of the walking of the Sunday School. He had beard many parties in the town say that they thought it would be better for the children to walk on the Monday, because they would then have the whole day. He should be glad to bear any suggestions from representatives of the Sunday' schools present.—Mr. A. JOLLEY' thought Tuesday would be the preferable• day for the children's procession, and he moved that it tske place on Tuesday the 21st of June.—The Rev.. J. YONGE ,asked whether, it, was desirable that the: Walking-Day of the childien should be changed!--1 Mr. BENNETT thought it there was to be two days'. holiday. it was desirable to stick to the original'! Walking Day, that "mai the Friday in Whit-week,— Mr. T. Jemmy-was in favour of having all the re- joicings on one day..—Mr. FUR,NBSS said behalf ofl Bewsey-street and SilVer-street Schools, that they were in favour• of merging Walking Day -with the I I Jubilee Day. He wished to know whether it was the intention of the Jubilee Committee te defray I the expense incurred by the, schools in connection with the Jubilee.—The MAYOR understood that each school had to.provide its own treat. —Mr. F2.llloNsca , did pot see where the treat came in if everbody had to provide for themselves. (Hear, hear, and laugh- ter.)—The Rev. J. YONGE thought that if the school fund and the general Jubilee fund were distinct there would.be a clashing of the two funds, and school managers would be launched in very great difficulties to raise money. Between the two stools he -was afraid-both would fall to thegromtd.—Mr. •T. BIRCHALL was in favour of the rejoicings all tak- I ing.Rlace on one day.—The Rev. S. WriacissoN -was ' also in-favour of One day. With regard to the pay- ment of childten'S tea he was in favour of its bning paid out of the Jubilee fund, but ,he had not at previous meetings proposed that as •he kneiv -he should have been beaten.—Mr. Moons pointed 'out that there was a lot of children who ditl hot 'attend Sunday schools.. The Salvationists generally looked I after these, but he did not know whether they I would ,do so this time or not. —The Rev. G.' E. Yorms Understood that .`.lie feeling of 'the managers a. Bold-street _school was in favour of one, dAy...—A delegate did not think it was advisible for the chil- dren to walk on the same day as the Trade and Friendly Societies.—Mr. F. Moxics said th'ey were, strong enough to have two days, and he suggested that the Trade and other societies should walk on the Monday and the children on the Tuesday.—Mr. S. DA.vras did not think they Would succeed if they had the demonstration all on one day, as many per- sons connected with the societies were also 'con- nected with the Sunday schools, and it would take all their time to look after the children.--ADEon- GATE of the Foresters said that Order were un- animously' in favour of the societies, Ste.. baying one day and the school children another. Trey sug- gested that Monday would • be the best dayefor the trades and' Tuesday for the children.—Mr. A. POTTER, onilehalf of the Shepherds, spoke to the same effect.—Mr. JUKES agreed with other speakers I that it would be impossible to have all the processions on one day, and he was in favour oftlie chil- dren walking on the Tuesday.—The Rev. J. WAn- NOCK (Presbyterian) said their school would be very glad to Jain in the procession on Meader, —Mr. F. MONKS then moved that the Jubilee celdbration be on two days, the trlae and friendly. societies on the first day and the Sunday schools on the oeCond day. Pbrran seconded this proposal.—Mr. T. JOLLEY- moved an amendment in favour of all taking place on one pay.—Mr.- T MORRIS suggested' that persons should.' give • in their names as guarantors for the expenses connected. with the Jubilee, and said he was willing to be a guarantor for fire per cent. (Hear, hear.)— 'The Misvon pointed out that 2150' had 'been already promided, awl gentlemen would bee appointed .to look after more fhnds.—After some further' Bisenasien the resolution was, carried unani- mously, -- Mr. Mors then proposed "That out of the jubilee fund a money payment- of 61' per head hs paid to the managers of the several Sunuay- schools taking, part in the.. demonstration, sucle names as are paid for to bs confrhed to those on the roll books on the 31st March." Mr. Monks pointed out that to allow 6rl perliead for 10,000,ehildren would 'only amount to £25.9; and to allow 24 per head for s treat to 1,000 old'people would amount to another £lOO, and le hadno doubt sulecient money- wouill be raisedto defray all those-expenses.--It 'was' mentioned by MiS.RerarirtnisT that the children who were looked after by the Saltration Army). and who attended Dallarn-lane ragged school would'be shut out from benefit, as their-names would' probably not appear on any roll book.—The MA-ron said the committee would be inclined to deal. liberally with cases of that kind.—After some farther discussion, Mr. MONKS altere&the latter part nftis resolution from, the "31st Mareh" to the "last Sunday in April."— The proposal' was then agreed to unanimously. —lt was next agreed; ore the motiOn of Mr. T. M'ONTILS, Seconded' by Mr. WEIGHT, that is 6d per head be alinwed for a treat to all old people over sixty years of age.- -After a little further discussion on matters of de- tail, it was. resolved, on the motion of M. Bram- yttrium seconded by 111r..8:R JontrsoN, that Messrs Barlow (treasurer). T..J01/ey-,../. Crosfieldl T. B. Car-. ter, F. Monks, and tire Mayor, be appointed co Finance Coramittee.—lt was also decided, on the, proposition of Mr. Parra% that a sub-committee be formed, to Consist 4 of' one delegate from each. Trade and Friendly Society.arid, on the -motion of Mr • LONGDIN, seconded* by Mr. T. BIROSALL, a sub-- committee was elaeted-tre consist of the superinten- dent-or secretary, or other delegate, of each Sunday. School.--On the suggestion of the Marou, seconded by MI% T. BTECHAtaI. it was resolved that the mom-. hereof the Finance Committee also constitute an Executive Committee, it being further resolvedthat the. question of-appointing a paid' secretary be left in the hands of'.the Executitge:Committee.—lt was also decided that the arrangements: for. a " feed " for the old people be left in the hands of ,1)11e Old People'S Treat Coreanittee.—The. Rector (the Rev. W. Quekett) wrots saying that be. hoped that, amidst-the multitude of suggestions, some permanent recollection of the Jubilee would be carried out,. He should be glad, he added, if Mr. Twist, onset his curates, could be placed' on the committee, as "he was well acquainted' with all matters of detail." It was decided to place the 'name of. Mr. Twist on the eommittee.—Another letter was received from Mr. H. Roberts, saying that he was unable to be present, but would take a share of the work. 4. Ile thought the question of granting a sum per head to each of the Sunday school's out of the Jubilee fund, to provide re- freshments was welt worthy of reconsideration, as than was a Strong feeling in the town thereon.

- - CB,ITPLE AND RAILWAY TELVELLING. —At the , Occasional Court House, Warrington, on Saturday, Yhomas I Henry), a cripple, without his right foot and left arm, and hailing from Leeds, was charged with travelling on the railway, without .tieket, from .4anchester to Earlestown. William Naylor, a -porter at the Earlestown station, stated that on the previous night on the arrival el the 10-5'5 p.m. train from Manchester, the prisoner was found concealed under the seat of one of the carriages. On being asked for his ticket he stated that he had DODO, an that he was making his way from Leeds to Liverpool, where he had an aunt, He was than given into the custody of the police.—The prisoner, in reply to the police, said he was born a cripple, and ' had been a clerk by profession, but he was now out of work. Be was trying to get to Liverpool, to his aunt, in the maurrer he was found. The prisoner was fined bs and costs, or iu default of pay- ment, seven days' imprisonment.

;TEXT OF THE CRIMES,BILL

The Central News on Saturday received an early copy of the bill--" to-make better provision for the-pre- vention and punishment of crime in Ireland, ancl.for other purposes-relating thereto." The following are the most Important clauses

PRELIMINARY INQUIRY., Clausel, Section I.—Where the Attorney-General for Ireland believes that any offence to which this section applies has been committed in a proclaimed district, he may (Erect a resident magistrate to hold an inquiry under this section,and thereupon such.resident magistrate may, although no person may be charged before him with the commission of such crime, sit at a police-court

or petty sessional court house of the police ~tation, and examine, on oath, concerning such offence, any witness appearing before him ;and may-take the deposition of such witness; and,if he has cause, may bind such wit- ness by recognisance to appear and give evidence at the next petty sessions, or when 'called upon vritifin three months from the date of such recognisance. A witness examined under this bill should not be ex- cused from answering any question on the ground that •the answer thereto May criminate or tend to criminate himself, but any statement made by any person, in Amer to any questions put to him on any examination' under this section, should not, except in the case of an indictment or other criminal proceeding for pejurv, be- admissible in evidence against him in any proceeding, civil or criminaL Clause 1, Section s.—The offencesto which this section applies are-any felony or misdemeanor, and any offence punishable-under this act.

SUM/WM .ItireLSDICTIOR, . Muse 2.—Any person who shall commit any of the following offences in a proclaimed district, may be prose- cuted before a court of Summary Jurisdiction under this Act: (1) Any person who shall take part in may criminal conspiracy to compel or induce any person or persons, either not to fulfil his-or their legal obligations or not to let, hire, use, or occupy any land, Of not to deal with, work for, or hire any person or persons in the ordinary course of trade, business or occupation, or to interfere with the administration of the law; (2) any person who shall wrongly and without legal authority use violence or intimidation (a) to or towards any person or persons, with a view to cause any person or persons either to do any act which such person or persons has or have a legal right to abstain from doing, or to abstain from doing, any act which such person or persons has or have a legal right to do, or (b) to or towards any persons in conse- quence either of his or their having done any act which he or they had a legal right to do, or of his ,or iheir having abstained from doing any act which he or they had a legal right to abstain from doing; 3, (a) any person who/ shall take part in any riot or unlawful assembly, or (b) within twelve months after the execution of any writ of possession of any house or land, shall wrongfully take or hold forcible possession of such house or land, or any part thereof, or (c) shall assault or wilfully and unlawfully resist .or obstruct any sheriff, constable, bailiff, process server' or other minister of the law, while in the execution of his duty,or shall assault him in consequenceof such execution; (4) any person who shall commit any offence punishable under the Whiteboy Acts, as defined by this Act; (5) any person who by words or acts &Hall incite, solicit, encourage, or persuade any other person to commit any of the offences hereinbefore mentioned. SPECIAL AIRY AND REMOVAL OF TRIAL, Clause 3.—Where an indictmentfora-crime committed in a proclaimed district has been found against a defen- dant, or a defendant has been committed for trial for

tion to and not In demgation of any. other powers or jurisdiction of arm court or authority sub- sisting atvommon law, or by Act of Parliament, m rela- tion-to such.trial, offence, or matter provided that no- person •should.be punished twice for the same offence. Clause 18.—An argreement or ' combination which under the Trade Union Acts, 1871 and 1876, or the Con- spiracy and Protection of Property Act, 1875, is legal, shall tnot, nor shall any act done in pursuance of any such agreement or combination, be deemed to be an offence against the provisions of this Act respectinrcon- :piracy, intimidation, and danverous associations. Clause_ 19 gives the definitions of the Act, and the thortatitle of the Act is set forth in Clause 20, as follows: —"This Act may be cited as the Criminal Law and Pro.i cedure(lreland) Act, 1887."

The laity of Maidstone have petitioned the Archbishop of Canterbury that Archdeacon flarrison's successor may be.chosen from the Maidstone clergy.
The Prince and Princess of Wales, accompanied by their daughters, left Marlborough House on Monday for Sandringham, where they spend Easter.

At Wadebridge, on Saturday., a boy named Pinch, 15, committed suicide by hanging himself. The jury found that be had done so from fear of his father, who hid threatened to break his neck. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone walked from Donis Hill to Willesden parish church on Sunday morning. Crowds of people assembled and witnessed the arrival and depar- ture of the right hon. gentleman.

On Saturday the Queen visited the villa at Cannes where the Duke of Albany died. Her Majesty also visited and conversed for a short time with Mr. Augus- tus Savile, who is dangerousic 1L At Hertfordshire Quarter Sessions, on Monday, the resignation of Lord Salisbury, as chairman, was accepted, with.a vote of thanks for his .past services. Lord Cowper was chosen his successor.

Mr, Irving, in accordance with his former observance of Holy week, closes the Lyceum theatre five nights this week, reopening on Saturday. evening, 9th inst. Mr. Irring's provincial tour, it LS now .understood, will commends in the middle of August.

• On Saturday morning, as the workmen engaged in constructing a bridge overthe railway at Sandiford, near Gaineborough, were lowering a heavy girder, weighing 7 tons, into position, the crane gave way and perciptated four men over the bridge into the cutting below. They were seriously injured, and the traffic was suspended for several, hours.

Tim-Sam CA.KATA—An influencial meeting, convened by the Mayor, was held on Monday in the Town Hall, Oldham, to further the Ship Canal scheme. Messrs. Platt. Moseley, and Bythell, directors of tlie Canal Com- pany, were present, and addressed the meeting. It was announced at the close that new shares to the amount of over £40,000 had been taken up in the room.

'Under the failure of Messrs. Stewart Bros., Canadian timber merchants,'Fen Court, and Bathurst, New Bruns- wick, in which the liabilities' are estimated at £150,000, and assets at £105,000, it was announced in the Bank- ruptcy Court on Monday, that The debtors had consented to an adjudication of bankruptcy, and it was resolved to appoint Mr. Kemp, Walbrook, trustee, with a committee of inspection. PROGRESS OF THE FORESTERS.—MT. ShaVICTOSS, the permanent secretary, has4just completed the statistics relating to the Ancient Order of Foresters. On the 31st December the Order consisted of 5,007 courts, with 667,750 financial members„an increase of 20,4193. during last year, with funds amounting to nearly four millions sterling. There are besides '15,652 honorary members, -who have increased by 735 during last year.

• CLERGY Dianalss Fenix—This fund now exceeds £20,000, and the first applications have been already dealt with substantial grants, in some cases aniounting to £2OO, being made where the circumstances of the clergyman applying were of an urgent nature. Many church collections have been promised during the spring and summer, and it is expected that the fund will re- ceive very large contributions from this source. ' At a meeting of 2,000 chainrnakers at Cradley Heath, on Monday, complaints were made that sections of the employers were-enforcing another reduction in wages. It was contended thatif this minority were.to rule the 5,000 chainmakers would be reduced to beggary and starvation. They must stop tyranny and trucking. It was unanimously resolved to call the whole of the branches of the trade out on strike 14 days hence.

- ROYAL Visrr To Setroan.—The Prince and Princess of Wales. in reply to a request made by the Mayor and Corporation of Salford, have announced that it 'will give them the greatest satisfactien to visit Salford on the morning of Wednesday, May 4th. Salford was evidently jealous of Manchester in the matter of the Royal visit, and their Royal Highnesses have willingly agreed to meet the wishes of the borough on the other side of the Irwell.

THE CREWE Mummut.—At Crewe Police Court on Mon- day Thomas Henry Bevin was again charged with the murder of his aunt, Mrs. Griffiths, in her own house, and with attempting to murder a little girl named Mary Jones' his cousin. There was little further evidence tendered, and the prisoner was again remanded. The girl, who was terribly beaten about the head, and who will be the chief witness, is progressing favourably, but she will not be able to attend court for some time to come.

111 E TOIXRVILLE CASE.—The petition of William Brigham, of Manchester, for the appointment of a re- ceiver of certain real estate in Yorkshire came before Mr. Justice Kay on Saturday. His Lordship stated that be had since lest Saturday seen the young Henry de Tour- vine, alleged to have been drowned in the Bay of Naples. The young lad, to whom the property belonged, would in future be under the court's ,protection. Re repro- bated the manner in which the petition had been pre- sented, and dismissed it with costs.

• A horrible prize fight took place, on Saturday, at a lonely spot several miles southcf Glasgow. The com- batants were James Flynn and William Taylor. The encounter lasted for over two hours, and BO rounds were fought. The fight was attended with varying success till the 30th round, when the excitement reached its zenith, and the blows were sickening. Flynn was fear- fully smashed, . and Taylor was hailed•vietor. A lot of money changed, hands on the result. The police never put in an appearance. Tun GREAT EAsTErin.—On Sundtey the Great Eastern was successfully awung in the River Liffey, at. Dublin, and started on bervoyage to Liverpool. The operation tasted about l'wo hours, and she moved down towards Poolbeg a".•• ix o'clock, it being then 'nearly high water. A crowd viewed her departure • from the 'quays. tugs assisted her, and she was brought out t,l' the port of Dublin by Mr. Peter Tallant, the same pilot who. had successfully taken 'her into it The weather was fine. Semen FISIITNIS BOATS AND CREWS Missiso.— Additional loss of life wAs reported on Saturday through the late gaie•ontheScotch coast A fishing boat which arrived at Buckie on Friday reportathat four men were washed overboard and drowned, and a boat which has arrived at Fraserburgh reports the loss of two lives in the same manner. Another boat, the Onward, of Rose- hearty, was passed on Friday bottom up, off Buchanan- ness. Her crew of six men have perished. Many boats are still missing, and, groat anxiety prevails among the • relatives of the crews. A 41c.An MOBEED.—A scene of extraordinary excite- ment •prevailed in the neighbourhood of St. John the Baptist Church, Liverpool, on Sunday, ctwing to the ritualistic dispute between the vicar, the Rev. Mr. Her- ring, and the parishioners. On leaving morning service the vicar was hooted and groaned by a crowd of 2,000 People. ire had to take refuge in the bridewell near the . church. The streets were sabsequentlyclearedby 60 police- men, and the vicar was escorted home by 20 policemen, a crowd following and hooting. A iraeas occurred in the church in the evening. On leaving the church the vicar took refuge in a passing tramcar, accompanied by seve- sal policemen, and a.scene similar to that of the Morning occurred outside. Eventually beseeched home in safety. Tare Stztarare, FRENCIINAN.—At;a late hour on Sunday, • Chauffat still remained in his .extraordinary prolonged sleep at the French cafe in Greek-street, Soho, London. 'A fire is kept constantly burning, in the room, and nourishment in liquid form is administered every two longs, the sleeper having first to be.arou.ted by a power- ful say of light being directed ;int) his, eyes. The 'patient was more easily aroused than en preceding days, and took milk anel bouillon very readily. On Monday it was stated 'that there had been a decided change for the better in the conditionaf Chauffat, and there were signs of his speedy recovery. He was more easily reused to take food, and readily obeyed the. doctor's requests. Dr. Reser says it is certain Chaaffat has not been drugged. Loss OF OVER SEVENTY LIVES ON THE SOOTCII COABT. —According to the latest accounts five boats' crews are stillmissing, sailing from Arbroath, Cellardyke, Fitten- weem, Lossiemouth, and Johnshaven, and the worst fears are entertained as to their fate. The Arbroath boat, the Ellen and Jane, had a. crew of six men, four married. The steam trawler Southesk, with 12 Arbroath fishermen on board, returned this forenoon ,after cruising 24 hours in search of the Agnes andlane,near the spot where she was last Seen, without result. The Cellardyke boat is the Snowdrop, skipper James Martin. She left Anstruther List Tuesday, and has not been heard of since. These were seven men on board, five of whom were married, and•leave large families: The Fittenweem boat is The Sisters. Her crew numbered seven.- The Lossiemouth boat is the Invincible, Alexander Scott skipper. The crew numbered eight hands, four of whom were married. The Johnshaven boat is the Martha, which was found abandoned and towed into Berwick. She had six hands altogether. It is a moderate computation to state that from 70 to 80 lives have been lost in this storm. ,

DEATH FROPI EATING PUTRID SAUSAGES AT SOUTHPORT. —OnTuesday, Mr.'W. T. Husband, deputycounty coroner, held an inquest at the Portland Hotel, Birkdale, South- port, on the body of Jane Welsh, four years of age, daughter of James Welsh, joiner, residing at 58, Kew- road.—Mrs. Welsh, the mother of the deceased, said that she, together with her husband and family, occupied apartments at the above address. On Thursday evening, M. Boyle, the landlady gave witness a quantity •of sausages, some of. which after being cooked, she gave to the children, and the rest to her hustand. The deceased, who was rather voracious, ate more than the other children, and shortly afterwards became ill and vomited a good deal. Next morning she was a atie better, but towards efening the grew worse. Witness sent for a doctor, but before his arrival the de- ceased expired. Noneof the other children felt any ill effects from eating the sausages. The 'deceased was la healthychild, and had no: had a day's illness since birth. So fares witness knewthere was nothing wrong with the sausages,—Mary Boyle, the landlady of the house, stated that about a forbiught ago she botzght 21b. of sausages at different shops. She cooked some of them for supper the same•evenit, and the remainder she kept till Thurs- day night, when she gave them, to Mrs. Welsh. The reason witness and her husband did not eat them was because it was Lent, and being Catholics they were for- bidden to partake of food of that description.—The jut-, after some consideration returned a verdict of "Death .by misadventure, throngkeating putrid sausages:*

.POLICE_IrLLIGENCE.
- - - WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Befere Alderman Harrison (in the chair), and

Councillor Oreening. MISCIELLANEOVS.—The following persons were fined fer drunkenness :—Bridget Foy and Mary Hanlon, in Glass- house-yard, fined 53 and costs each; Margaret Ford, on Cropper's-brow, fined ss, including costs; Martin Carley, on Friar's-green, fined 53 and costs; Edward Crosfiy, in Buttermarkw-street, sentto prison for fourteen days.—Rn- pert Wilson, for conamittlng a breach of the peacety fight- ing, was bound over to be of good behaviour for six months, in his own recognisances of £s.—Annie Mahar was fined lOtt and costa for using obscene language on the 22nd ult., ill Battersby-lane. 'Frederick Hunt and John Griffiths, youths, were each fined 10. and costs for playing at football to the danger of the passengers in Birchall-street, on thit 27th ult., and, for a similar offence in John-street, a little lad named John Dickenson was fined is. including costs.-- For keeping a dog without a license Thomas Smith WU fined 108 and costs.

ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A PONY.—Henry Brandwood, a youth, was summoned for ill-treating a pony on the 261 k ult., and William Beswick was summoned as the owner, for causing the animal to be no worked. Mr. A. Browne ap- peared for the defence. It was alleged that the pony wag saffering from a wound. In defence it ,was stated that the horse had been kept up until the wound was nearly healed, and also that Mr. Beswick was unaware that it was being worked. The magistrates dismissed the case on payment of costs. _

DRAWING A PENSION.—Martin Cassidy. of Ashton, a pensioner, was charged with haying been drunk in Mersey- street, early on Sunday morning. When apprehended de. - fendant had -.£2 13s in his possession, audit was stated that defendant bad on Saturday drawn his pension. It was hg twenty-second appearance. Fined 5s and costs. TRUNTSFER.—The license of the Gardeners Arms, Brick. street, was temporarily transferred from Richard Price to Gilbert Cook, an off-license of a shop in Hoyle-street being transferred from Gilbert Cook to Miss Cook.

Scaoot CASES.—The following parents were summoned by Mr. Riley for not sending their children regularly to school, and were dealt with in the usual manner :—Richard Critchley, tool maker, Pocket-street; John Rooney, stoke:, Crosley-street ; Peter Farrell, labourer, Ship-yard and Patrick Clark, cab driver, Latchford. TITESDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton and Mr. E. J. Guest
DRUNKENNESS—For havingbeen drunk in Dial-street on the previous evening, Benjamin Box was fined 5s and costs.
WEDNESDAY.- Before Mr. John Fairclough, Alderman Chandley, Councillors Greening and Frartcoutb. and Mr R. Garnett. .

DISORDERLY Womm—Catherine and Mary Connolly, who received very bad characters, were each sent to prisoft for a month for baying been drunk and disorderly in Rose- yard on Tuesday.—Selina Jones, for having been drunk and - guilty of indecent conduct, was also sent to prison for &- month.

BID Boys.—Three boys named Patrick Fallon, John Stanton, and Whittaker, were charged with frequenting the entrance to Bank Quay Station with intent to commit a . felony., Fallon had previously been convicted of breaking into Heath-aide School, which schbol was again broken int* on the morning previous. The lads lived by thieving. The Bench dismissed them with a caution.

CRUELTY TO A Holism—John Tayle.'', of Hindley, waft. sammoned for ill-treating a mare on the 29th ult.—lnspec— tor Aplin, R.S.P.C.A., gave evidence showing that he saw' the defendant in Bridge-street le charge of two horses which were attached to a cart laden with rabbirg storms. The horses were in ft miserable condition, and there were several wounds on their less and body.—Sergeant Bowen having • corroborated this evidence, the magistrates imposed a fine of 5s and costs.

Thuitepay.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. MISGELLANEOUS.—JobG Arthur Jones, a young man, was charged with being in possession of military clothing—a shirt, braces, socks, end boots--without being able to give , a satisfactory account of how he obtained the same. Pri- soner said he bought the articles from a tramp ; he did not know that they were military articles. A rine of 20s and costs, or one month's imprisonment, was imposed.— Mabel Gandy, for being drunk and disorderly in Bridge. street, was sent to prison for 14 days.—Robert Mulholland was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly In Mersey-street, on the 2nd Inst. Fined 5s and costs.—Wm. Cassidy, charged with having been drunk in Knutsford. - road, was fined 5s and costs.— George Morton, Mary Knock- - ton, Michael Gough, Robert Dakin (72nd appearance) were each fined for similar offences ; and Bridget McDonough was sent to prison for 14 days. ALLEGED Cnunray.—Charles Cook, a boy, was sum- moned for ill-treating a horse on the 2nd just, and George Grange, the owner, was summoned for having cansed it to be so treated by allowing it to be worked while in an unfit condition. It was stated that the horse had been destroyed, and the case was dismissed on payment of costs. BREACH OF TrIE PEACE.—William Kelley and JitEleff Rabbit were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Bridge-street on the Ist instant. They were each ordered to find a surety for their good behaviour for six months, or go to prison for seven days.—Williana Donoghue and Thomas Oaks were summoned for fighting in Bridge-street. Donoghue was ordered to be bound over, . and Oaks was dismissed.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. P. Stubs (in the chair) and

• Z. Armitage. RATING CASE.—James Berry was summoned that he be. log a person duly rated and assessed for land in the town. ship of Woolston had refused to pay Is 2d rates and is 61 arrears, and a distress warrant was asked for.—Mr. Robert Davies appeared for the defence.—Mr. Houghton, overseer, said the rate and arrears which had been demanded were for land at Woolston Moss, over which defendant had the right of shooting. He had planted the land with trees some years ago and it was used for the purpose of harbouring game. Before making the assessment the kundary; which had existed for some 30 or 40 years, was taken and was not disputc d.—ln AllBWer to the Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Nichol. • eon), Witness said that part of the Moss was enclosed. and. Mr. Berry was the visible tenant.—Evidence was also given.. to the effect that Mr. Berry's keepers bad taken gentlemen on to the land to shoot game.—Mr. Robert Davies contended that there was nothing to rate upon the land—neither game nor trees. Again, there was not one portion of the land assessable in the township.—Defendant gave evidence,firt the course of which he denied that he owned or occupied any, land in the township. His mother.io-law, Mrs. Mary Ann Jackson, of Pendlebury, owned land in the township, and he had shot over It, and might have gone on to it. The game had never been severed from the land, therefore it was not rateable.—The magistrates.considering that Mr. Berry was net proved to be the owner or occupier, refused to grant the application for a distress warrant.

Mis.Cuzainous —James Orford and Patrick McGee, labourers, were ordered to pay costs for having been drunk and disorderly at Poulton.—James Scarisbrick, charged with a similar offence at Woolston, was fined fie and costs. —John Riley, fruiterer, was summoned for cruelty te a horse at Eariestown on the 11th of February by working it whilst in an unfit condition.—Fined 15s, including costs. —A boy named Frank Kelly was charged by William Gorse with stealing a muzzle, value is 31, his property, on the 23th nit.—Prisoner and other boys were playing with the dog at Ciolborne, and later on its muzzle was missed.— Prisoaer said two 13,5y8 told him to take the muzzle off the dog, and to sell it. —Prosecutor did not wish to press the case, and prisoner was discharged on his father promising to whip him.--Abel Stretch was summoned for being drunk on the licensed premises of Edwin James Davies, the Butchers' Arms, Great Sankey, on the 14th ult., and or- dered to pay the costs.—Henry Barber, contractor, of Warrington, was summoned for having two carts at Pen- keth in use without his name being legibly painted :hereon. —Fined Is and coats in each case.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MoNnay.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. G. L. Davies. _ _ _

rERMISBION TO SELL.—Joseph Bancroft, WB5 granted tern- porary authority to sell at the Queen's Head, Waterton Road: Danux.—Thomas Blairemore and David Phillips, were each fined 10s and coats for being drunk and disorderly in Fryer-street on tte 24th Mara.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
_ _ --• MONDAY—Before Messrs Holbrook Gaskell, jun., and John Brock.

Hamm AGAM—Thomas Haynes, a youth of Newtown, was fined 8s and costs, or seven days' in default, for haying ' been drunk and disorderly in Victoria-road on Saturday night.—P.C. Coupe proved the offence.—Margaret Jones, a married woman of Water-street, for haying been drunk In that thoroughfare on Saturday night, was fined a similar sum. The offence was proved by P.C. Coats. FRUITING Womms.—Margaret Wall, a married woman, of Caroline-street, for creating a breach of the peace by fighting with another woman on Saturday night, was bound over to keep the peace for three montbe--berself in the sum of £lO, and two suteties of £s—or ten days in default. MORE BEGOING.—Willinn Richards, for begging in Birchfield•road on &today, was committed to gaol for seven days' bard labour —William Edwards, a youth, was com- mitted to gaol for a like term for begging on the same day. in Parsonage-road

div.p: a Federal constitution it would still be the Imperial Parliament, when representatives of the other parts of the kingdom were called to its deliberations. The English Parliament would be summoned for English purposes in an English session, and in an Imperial session for Imperial purposes, at which latter Irish, Scotch, and Welsh representatives would be present. The Imperial Parliament thus constituted, relieved from the embarrassment of local affairs and free to move in its own elevated sphere, would be able to do more for the Empire in one short session of two or three months than it can now attempt in a series of years. Ireland would be contented, or obliged to consume her discontent at home, which would be the next best thing for Eng- land; her people, like those of Scotland and Wales, would be fully occupied in attending to their own business, and the union of the United liingdom would be stronger than ever. We need hardly say that we cordially endorse the above enunciation of opinion ; and we are so strongly conVincd that the way out of the Irish bog lies in this direction that we should like to have the views of pur readers on the subject. We therefore invite criticism from Liberals, Liberal Unionists, and Tories : for'we do not see why the scheme should not commend itself to politicians of all shades. The Liberal Unionists who favour it are apt, so far as our observation has gone, to com- mend it as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S plan; but it should be noted that it involves something more than provincial assemblies with purely administrative functions. These Home Rule Parliaments would have large legislative powers ; there wonld in fact be separate legislation for each nation in harmony with the habits, instincts, and aspirations of the people of each country. It would be a case of sub-division of labour on a national and consequently a natural basts. There may be grave objections to such a plan ; but if there are we must confess that we are not familiar with them; and if the proposal is, as we be- lieve it to be, one which will least divide the country, the sooner it is discussed and brought into operation, the better it will be for the United Kingdom.

LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL'S explana- tion to his constituents, on Saturday, as to his reasons for resigning his post as Chancellor of the Exchequer, read like a chapter of ancient history —so rapidly have events marched within the past few months. His lordship would appear to have felt this, for, when he tound he could not rouse his audi- ence on the question of finance, he proceeded to devote the greater portion of his speech to Home Rule and the Government Coercion Bill. He supports the measure—" every pro- vision of it "—and he warns the Government that "if they are weak about the bill, if they make any concessions on any ofie point, they will get upon the road to a lot of concessions, and the bill will not be passed, and the Union will be lost." Lord RANDOLPH knows better, than most people that this is the veriest nonsense; but it serves his purpose to talk in this strain. He finds that the Government have not collapsed, as he expected they would when his support was withdrawn; that the Liberal Unionists are bent upon trying coer- cion ; and that, if he is not to he utterly effaced during the present Parliament, he must go with the current, even when, as he prob- ably foresees, it will terminate in shipwreck. There has been considerable speculation in certain quarters as to the possibility of the mem- ber for South Paddington crossing over to the Liberal side of the House; but we have not been amongst those who have ever thought he would take that course. In politics it is a question with him of the advancement of a person rather than a principle, and that per- son is himself. He is discerning enough to perceive that, whilst he is a great man amongst the little men of the Tory party, he would be a little man amongst great men if he joined the ranks of the Liberals. lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has no desire to dwarf himself; he would rather got upon some- body's shoulders in order to be seen. His speech on Saturday centres upon self from beginning to end. The Government, thanks to the Liberal Unionists, are not likely to col- lapse for the present ; so his lordship, since he has failed to block their`path, has made up his mind to assist in hurrying them on to destruction. He speaks of Lord SALIS- BURY as a great man, and we may be quite sure that he will be avenged at the earliest opportunity for being thus compelled to pay compliments of this kind. He knows per- fectly well that the PRIME MINISTER is de- lighted with his being out of the way, and, for a time, iet any rate, reduced to impo- tence. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has obviously miscalculated the strength of the forces that were at work When he resigned the Government were in despair ; it was thought that he would either soon be back, having dictated terms, or that the SALISBURY Administration would shortly be numbered amongst the filings of the past. There was just then fair prospect of re-union amongst the Liberals; Lord RANDOLPH be- lieved it was near at hand ; and knowing the life of the Government would not, after that event, be worth a month's purchase, he deemed it of little moment whether he was in the Cabinet or out when the crash came. The failure of the Round Table Conference has naturally changed the situation on every side. It has made Lord HARTINGTON for the time being more than ever master of the situation; and given, in all probability, a new lease of life to the SALISBURY Adminis- tration. There is no love lost between Lord HARTINGTON and Lord RANDOLPH; and it is not, therefore, unlikely that the member for Rossendale has taken a special interest in the work of assisting the Ministers to hold together without the aid of the member for South Paddington. "Rip VAN WINKLE" was looked upon alike by Lord RANDOLPH and by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN as a slow sleepy sort of fellow ;. but they have both got to dance just now to his piping. This sort of unnatural alliance will not, of course, be lasting; "it is not and it cannot come to good ;" but that is no reason why those who have an eye for the incongruous should not enjoy the humour of the situation.

NEW MAGISTRATES FOR CHESHIETC-At the Che- shire Quarter Sessions, on Monday. the following gentlemen qualified as magistrates for the county: —Francis Thorneley, Birkenhead; Stephen Chesters Thompson, Higher Ardwick, Manchester; Thomas Ward, Northwich ; Richard Hobson, Bromborough ; William Wycliffe Barlow, Wilmslow; Thomas Comber, Leighton, near Park Gate; Reginal Bushell, Neston. C4,HURCII AND CHAPEL SITES.—" The Bishop of Lichfield has been trying to play in the Lords the same shabby little trick which Mr. Powell is at- tempting in the Commons. One ground on which the bill for the compulsorypurchase of sites for dis- senting places of worship is advocated is, that the Church of England already has that power u h . yTtheant, say these two worthies, let the Church give power; because, as the Bishop naively says, it has influence enough to obtain land without it. But, replied Lord Kimberley, the grievance complained of by Nonconformists would still exist—viz., that they are not allowed to erect places of worship in many places where the land is owned by Church- men. That inequality would, as Lord Herschell said, remain; and even the House of Lords saw that, and so rejected the Bishop's bill without a division,"—The Likrator.

"Easter Holiday! Humph," says the Old Fogey who has a touch of rheumatism, "and the wind is in the east; it is always in the east; but at this time of the year it is very much so —it is Easter."

Earlestown has this week been treated to an excellent exhibition of gas cooking, heat- ing, and labour-saving appliances. It is a capital field for a movement of this kind, for—note this, inhabitants of other towns— the price of gas is zs, 3d. per thousand only. That is something like an inducement to con- sumers.
