The Warrington Town Council have "been and gone and done it;" they have put four- pence in the pound on the rates for the com- ing year. Are they trying to break the camel's back with the last straw? Perhaps, as the Council was all but silent, our readers may have something to say. We intend having another word on the subject ourselves next week.

THE WEST LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CUP.—The final tie took place at St. Helens on Thursday evening between Pemberton and Widnes St. Mary's club. The latter, who were considered in the locality to have a good chance of winning the trophy, had to accept defeat to the extent of 16 points to nil. FAILURE OF A WIDNES GROCER.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Monday a receiving order was granted by Mr. Registrar Bellringer. on the petition of Mr. George Bedgood, baker and grocer, 12 and 14, Albert-road, Ap,tleton, Widnes. The petition was flied on behalf of the debtor by Mr. T. J. Peters, solicitor, Widnes. Foornim, : PUBLICANS V. TRADESMEN.—Much interest was manifested yesterday in a gem., of football played on the Widnes ground, between a team cemposed of puelicane and a team of tradesmen. Tbedionifeces proved the victors by three tries and three minors to four minors. Mr. H. C. Speakman, of Runcorn, was the referee. WIDNES THEATRE BOYAL.—The successful drama "Man to man" has been presented at this place of entertainment during the past week by Mr. William Browne' s company, under the management of Mr. Herbert Budd. The piece teems with dramatic Incidents and exciting situations, while the dialogue is interesting and well sustained through- out by a very strong cast The scenic effec s are a capital feature in the performance. VISIT OF THE BLUE HUNGARIAN BAND TO RUNCORN.—On Wednesday and Thursday evenings next week the people of Runcorn will hive an opportunity of listening to the clever performances of the Blue Hungarian Band, which achieved such great popularity at the Liverpool Exhibition last summer, and hen recently been filling the Bijou Opera House, Liverpool, with delighteo audiences. NEW MANUFACTURE AT RUNCORN.—After being idle for nearly two years, tee Glycerine Works on the Sprinch aro to be re-opened shortly by Messrs. Hughes Brothers, of Liverpool, as a lird refining manufactory. Mr. h. Buck has been appointed local agent and traveller to the firm, and new machinery haying been already introduced into the works, operations may be expected to commence in a few weeks. At the beginning employment will be found for about 30 men. WIDNES GYMNASIUM HARRIERS.—Sixteen members of this club had an agreeable eight-mile run on Saturday. They left the Millfield Inn at 3-30, and proceeded by Appleton village, over the lielde, past the Four-topped Oak, to Crou- ton. The afternoon was b4aUtifllity tine, and the outing was quite enjoyable. The patty reached borne, after a spirited finish as usual, at about 4-30. P. McMahon was first by I half-a-dozsn yards ; F. Franklin was second, and G. Ether- idge third, G. and R. Evans and Jack Roscoe being their nearest e,tendents. The others finished indiscriminately. SACRED CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—Runcorn Public Hall was well filled Oil Sunday evening by an audience assem- bled to listen to a sacred concert given by the members of the Tonic Sol-fa Choir, which has been organised by Mr. John Holford. Without the aid of instrumental music the choir rendered a number of part-songs on sacred themes in a manner that gave much pleasure to those present, and reflected great credit upon the ability and training of the vocalists. Mr. P. Richardson, of Liverpool, sang two solos, one by Crounod and one by Handel, in good style. He was accompanied on the piano by Mrs. W.B. Kay.

The Warrington Jubilee Committee are acting wisely in arranging to have two pro- cessions—one of Trades and Friendly So- cieties on the Monday, and the other of school children on the Tuesday. One big procession might end in a big failure; it would certainly prove monotonous to adults, and tiresome to children. Besides, the arrange- ment gets over. the difficulty of the real and the official Jubilee day ; and • makes cock- sure of two holidays.

Second thoughts are best, too, in the mat- ter 'of allowing out of the Jubilee Fund sixpence a head for each scholar to provide school treats. This is better than soliciting separate subscriptions for each school as in the case of Walking Day. Knowing that they will not be solicited this year for the Walking Day contributions, subscribers will feel called on, of course, to give more freely to the Jubilee Fund.

The police of St. Helens and the neigh- bourhood hav-! been making a raid upon offenders against the law for the regulation of explosives ; and the result is startling. There seems to be as much gunpowder and dynamite "lying about" in unregistered places as would blow half the inhabitants into eternity. The magistrates seem to think that in most cases it was "all a mistake." , The rule for the present is one of small fines; when a J.P. has been killed by mistake the fines will be increased.

The magistrates of Runcorn are tender towards offenders against the regulation as to keeping dogs under control. On Mon- day they imposed several fines of sixpence; but, as they carried 9s. 6d. in the shape of costs, most people will think that the penalty was sufficiently high. A Widnes woman was pounced upon for having hr dg with her at Runcorn; but she urged that "both the dog and cat followed her from home." There was no resisting such a plea, so the Bench dismissed the case.

RUNCORN WESLEYAN METHODIST SUNDAY SCHDOL Umos.—The annual meeting of this Union of schools in the Runcoin circuit was held in Brunswick School on Tuesday night. There was a capital attendance, represen- tatives being present from various parts of the circuit. After tea, the Rev George Ward took the chair, and Mr. S. Pope read the Union r-part," while the Inspectors' report was read by Mr. J. Uneworth. Both reports were passed without discussion, in order to allow the Rev. C. H. Kelly, of London, ncre,ary to the Wesleyan Sunday School Union, to deliver an address. The remarks of the rev. gentleman were attentively listeked to, and the meeting closed with the customary votiis of thanks. RUNCORN AND THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE.—The cemmittee appointed to consider the best mode in which to celebrate the Jubilee of the Queen have held a meeting, and dis- cussed the various schemes suggested at the public gather- ing of the townspeople. The general feeling of those pre- sent was in favour of the organisation of a processisn of friendly societies and Sunday schools, and it was decided to issue a circular to the officials of the various institutions on the subject. This scheme, if carried out, will include the provision of a tea for the children not connected with a school, and for the old and infirm people. On Tuesday night the members of the Co-operative Society will meet to discuss what financial aid they will give to the Jubilee celebrations.

Thomas Clarke, a grocer in a small way of business at Prescot, has been called upon to pay 2IS for selling adulterated pepper. The foreign element was found to be ground olive stones. What will they mix next ? You ask for pepper, and are supplied with olive stones. Clarke professed his inno- cence, sayinz he got th?, " pepper " from Liverpool. This is likely enough, and it is to be hoped the police, having landed the Prescot minnow, will now set about the cap- ture of the Liverpool leviathan.

A contemporary is good enough to inform the world that " Ladies' under garments are now composed of very fine cambric, dotted with small designs, such as horse-shoes, tre- foils, Szo., in scarlet or marine blue." "It is well to have something nice," as the old lady said when selecting a pattern for a night cap, " in case of fire, or an earthquake, you know." But as to these " small designs" for undergarments—is it not just possible that there might be a failure to observe the " horse shoes, trefoils, ttc.," in case of an earthquake. ?

GOOD FRIDAY AT RUNCORN A. 1.713 WIDNES.—There was a general cessation from labour in these towns yesterday. There were services at the churches of the estab- lishment, and at the Cithol ic Chapels, but the majority of the inhabitants took advantage of the holy day to go in search of pleasure. Early in the morning two trips departed from Runcorn for the watering places on the Welsh coast, and a fair number of passengers were booked. Afterwards the station was closed as on Sundays, and people who wished to go far afield had to traverse the Bridge to Widnes. Large numbers, however, went by road to Frodsham and Chester. The railway traffic at Widnes was very heavy, the chief places patronised being Black- pool, Southport, Liverpool, and Manchester, and the rural spots nearer home, such as Hale, Fiddlers Ferry, and Lynam. At both Runcorn and Widnes several of the Nonconformist denominations held tea parties and entertainments. The weather was fine, but a cold wind blew from the north- Widnes v. Sefton.—The return match be- tween the above teams was played on Saturday, at Hough Green' resulting in a victory for the home team by 4 goals to 2. The first match this season resulted in a victory for Widnes ter 5 goals to nil, though they only played 11 men to their opponents' 12. On Saturday last Widnes were again short, playing ten men to Sefton's eleven. The home team lost the toss, and had to play against the sun and a stiffish breeze for the firsthalf. In spite of this, however, they were the first to score, by means of a good shot by Wylde. Sefton then played up, and Day scored twice for them, Sefton thus leading by two goals to lat half-time. With the wind in their favour Widnes peppered the Sefton goal continually during the second half, but chiefly owing to the good defence game of J. Halsall, they were only able to score 3 goals, the final score being four goals to two. With this match the Widnes season has terminated with 9 victories and 6 defeats. They have scored 45 goals (to which H. Wilson and J. Wylde have contributed 18 and 9 res- pectively) to their opponents 43. FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. EVANS AT RUNCORN. The remains of Mr. Richard Evans, formerly manager of the Mersey-road (Widnes) branch of the Runcorn Co-epera- ties Society were interred at Runcorn Cemetery on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Evans died on Friday night, the first inst., after only a WPSE'S illness, and the greatest sympathy is felt for his widow, who was made a bide the brief period of four months ago. A useful worker in St. John's Presby- terian Sunday School, superintendent of the Juvenile Teat of the Independent order of Rechabites, and a leading mern• ber of the Blue Ribbon Gospel Army, Mr. Evans was much respected, and the demonetntion at his funeral was of an imposing character. Preceding the body were the members of the committee of the 'Runcorn Co-operative Society, and the whole of the employees of that body, and then came in the order named the members of the Union Tent of Recha- bites, representatives of the Life Boat Crew Division of the Order of Sons of Temperance; the members of the Union Juvenile Tent, the members of the Blue Ribbon Army, and many members of the congregation of St. John's Presby- terian Cnapel. The coffin' upon which were placed a num- ber of wreaths, was borne by several members of St. John's Chapel. Notwithstanding the boisterous state of the weather, a large crowd of people assembled at the cemetery to witness the last sad rites, which were performed by the Rev. E. Williams and the Rev. E. Jones. THIS POPULAR CONCERTS AT RUNCORN. The Mill Brow Military Band had a "bumper house" on the occa- sion of the last of the series of popular concerts held in Bethesda Schoolroom, on Tuesday evening. Although the earlier enterteinments would not add much to the coffers of the band, the members of which have attained more than a local reputation as musicians, perseverance has produced success, and on the whole the season has been an eacourag- ing one. The programme presented on Tuesday evening , was of more than usual merit, and the audience were net slow to signify their approval. Miss Fanny Bouffieur, of Liverpool, by her sweet and expressive vocalisation, proved that the favourable feelings she excited on her first visit were not misplaced. and she had to respond to an enthusias- tic encore. Mr. Percy Barton, the tenor, was equally SRC. cessful, and the humorous songs and sketches of Mr. Wil- son Blackledge formed a hugely diverting portion of the programme. Miss Pierpoint, of Runcorn, also appeared in conjunction with Miss Bouffieur and Mr. Percy Barton in the trio "0 ! memory." Mr. Tom Outhwaite, to whom the band owes much for his painstaking instruction, per- formed a euphonium sole with his customary skill. Mrs W. B. Kay ably officiated as accompanist. In conclusion it must be stated that the tasteful performances of the band were highly appreciated, and it is to be hoped that now the summer season is approaching the inhabitants will again have an opportunity of listening to their strains of harmony ha the open air.

Councillor Bolton and Councillor Dixon are quite justified in pointing to the glaring inequalities which exist in the appointments of members of the Warrington Town Council to the various committees. Councillor F. A. Roberts was appointed to fill the seat left vacant by the death of the late Councillor Broadbent ; and it is customary in other towns, under similar circumstances, to allow the newly-elected councillor to occupy some, if not all, of the vacant seats in committee. We can scarcely credit the statement that Mr. F. A. Roberts was not, until Tuesday last, on a single committee. If this be so, it is a dis- credit to the Corporation.

Mr. Arch presented a petition against the return of Lord Henry Bentinck for North- West Norfolk; and proved that his lordship, after the election, had sent a postal order for £3 to an elector as, in the words of the writer, "a little present, as some small com- pensation for all the trouble and worry you have had in connection with the election, and 9.fterwards." And yet the petition failed; it was ruled that this was not a breach of the provisions of the Corrupt Practices Act. Lord Henry seems to know his way about in mak- ing "a little present" to an elector. He will probably have a numerous following in the way of imitators at the next election.

After the first feeling of indignation against the Speaker for permitting the application of the Closure, on Saturday, Liberals are dis- posed to feel sorry for him. The fact is the Government have made a mull of it by im- posing upon the Speaker the necessity of seeming to become a partizan of whatever Ministry happens to be in office. If he had vetoed the application Mr. Smith made as leader of the House, it would have been looked upon as an insult to the Government. As it is, it is regarded in some quarters as an insult to the leader of the Opposition. This is not as it should be; the rule is a bad one which is thus liable to impale the first Commoner in England on the horns of a dilemma.

THE QUEEN'S AIDES-DE-CAMP.— Lord Gerard's death has left a vacancy among the Queen's aides- de-camp. He was appointed some years -ago to re- present the Yeomanry branch of the auxiliary forces, from which service his successor will have to be chosen. The Peerage is well represented on the list of Queen's aides-de-camp. The Militia list in- cludes Lord Winmarleigh, Lord Methuen, Lord Exeter, Lord Stanley, Lord Meath, Lord Lovat, and Lord Oxenbridge ; in the Yeomanry list we have Lord Eversleigh, Lord Warwick, the Duke of West- minster (also a Volunteer), and Lord Fitzwilliam ; whilst the Volunteers gave Lord Wemyss, Lord Bury, Lord Ilardinge, and Lord Truro.

LOGS AT LARGE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Ses• sions. oa Monday, George Maddison, of Appleton-in•Wid• nes, was summoned for allowing his dog to be at large on the 23rd March. PC. Povey proved the case, and a fins of 6d, and costs Os td, was imposed.—Alice Mellor, of Wid- nes, was summoned for a like offence committed in Than- tyre-street on the 26th March. P.C. Povey proved the case. The defendant said she had only just come over the bridge, and knew nothing of the order to keep dogs under control. Both the dog and cat followed her from home. The Bench, as the order had only thee been in force a few days, disinissed the case.—Arthur Povey, Suffolk-street ; Joseph Savage. butcher, Greenway•road ; Loftus Don, an actor; Thomas Povey, Halton; Isaac Speakman. chemist, Bridge-street, were each fined 6d and costs on similar charges of having their dogs at large on various dates.—Sain eel Cox, carter., was charged with not having his dog under control. His defence was that he had given the dog to a person at Widnes. The dog returned and he fastened it in the stable, whence it subsequently escaped. The case woe distnissed.—Thomas Saunders, of Church-street, was tined 63 and costs for allowing his dog to he at large. LOTTERIES AT IiIINCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions OR L Monday William Thomas and Charles Knock, were charged with keeping a lottery in the Public Market. Both defend- ants pleaded guilty, but stated that they were unaware they were committing an offence. Supt. Hollingworth said the men were brought up under an old Act of Parliament, and they were liable to be dealt with uuder the vagrancy Act as rogues and vagabonds. P.C. Smith described the operations of the prisoners. On Saturday night Thomas bad a small stall on the market ground. His stock in trade consisted of a number of small blue packages each containing a ring and occasionally in the sight of the nelsons assembled the prisoner would put a threepenny piece, and sometimes two into a packet. He sold a great many packages, the great majority of which simply contained a ring. The Constable purchased a packet, which contained a ring, and the prisoner said' If you had taken this one you would have had 6d " and he took ups package and displayed two threepenny pieces. At the police station the constable searched the prisoner and found in his possession LI 5s In his box were about 200 packages, but in this large num- ber only one threepenny piece could be found. An hour afterwards Constable Smith saw the prisoner Knock carrying on a lottery. He displayed a considerable number of dolls, necklaces, pipes, and other articles of small value; and sold packets at the rate of two for a penny each containing a ring or a breastpin, occasionally one would contain a ticket en- titling the lucky purchaser to some article on the stall. The constable purchased a couple of packets, and received a ticket entitling him to a fancy horn. Scores of persons however purchased packets but received no prize. When appreberided Knock was searched by Inspector Millington, who found upon him £2 5s 8. Inspector Hollingsworth said this practise was being put down in other parts of the country, and he asked the Bench to do likewise. In carry- ing out the act the police had a difficult duty to perform. On Saturday night the people thought the constable was exceeding his duty. The Bench fined each defendant £1 and costs 5s 10d. The Magistrates declined to confiscate the property of the prisoners.

THE ANTROBUS GRAVE DISPUTE.—At Northwich County Court,, on Wednesday, before his Honour I Judge Ffoulkes, a case was beard in which Isaac Johnson and Son, monumental stone masons, of Kelsall, near Northwich, were plaintiffs, and William Robinson, farmer, Antrobus, was defendant. Mr. Fletcher (Northwich) appeared for plaintiffs, and Mr. P. Davies (Warrington) for the defendant. The claim was for a gravestone supplied by plaintiffs, which was erected by them in Antrobus churchyard, and was for the sum of £9. Witnesses were called to prove that a gravest one was erected by the order of defendant, and that it was copied from a design previously agreed upon. For the de- fence Mr. Davies said that the headstone was not at all like the design, and remarked that the defend- ant said the stone supplied was not of the quality that it should have been. His Honour held that the stone was not according to the order given, and gave judgment for the defendant, with costs., GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD. On Tues- day the monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Schools. There were present Messrs. Turner (chairman), Houghton, Ridgway, Kerfoot, and Cook; S. Sutton (Clerk). The Clerk said that the total balance in favour of the Board in the hands of the treasurer was £lO3 Os 10c1. It was also stated by the Clerk that he had received from the Education Department a com- murication on the subject of the proposed new schools at Sankey Bridges. It stated that the Edu- cation Department had written twice to Mr. Sum- mersg,ill, of Sankey Bridges, requesting him to state the reasons why the proposed schools had a claim to be placed on their lordships annual grant list, but they had received no reply andit was presumed that the proposal had accordingly dropped. Should it be revived, however, the School Board would again be communicated with.—The Chairman : That is satisfactory.—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Hughes of Sankey, in which he stated that: efforts were being made to obtain new premises for a Sunday School for St. Mary's at Sankey, and on be- half of the Committee he asked whether the Board would be willing to grant the use of the Board ' School during the year for concerts, tea meetings, ' &;c.—The Chairman said they would have no chili- culty in granting that application subject to the schools being left in proper condition, &c. The , only other business before the Board was the con- sideration of a few cases of non-attendance of children at the school.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. P. Speakman. Pre- sent—Messrs. Dobson, Grice, Hankheson, Aleadowcroft, Imison, Mellor, Whittaker, Lake, Lighthurn, Fisher, and Pritchard ; W. Marshall (secretary), and Barker (sur- veyor).

div.head: SHIP . CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP . CANAL.

Mr. Lightburn asked the chairman if he intended to use the weight of the Board of Commissioners in advoca- ting the claims of .the ship canal. The struggling shop- keepers and worlusgmen would benefit largely by the scheme, and he did not know a single individual who would suffer through the construction of the canal. It ought to be impressed upon the public that those who took up shares would not have to pay anything except on allotment, And that there would be no allotment until the construction of the canal was assured. Therefore, if the canal was not pro- ceeded with, there would be no claim upon them.—The Chairman said this matter hardly came within the province
rof the Board.—Mr. Lightburn said he was aware at that, but be wished the members to throw their influence into the* matter. There was DO other business.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Present Mr. J Pritchard, chairman, Dr. McDou- gall, Messrs F A Lake, S C Beckett, E Imison, and F Rigby (Clerk).

ME. LAKE. The Clerk read a letter received from Mr F A Lake, who withdrew t..e notice of his intention to resign his position as a member of the Board. THE FINANCIAL POSITION. The Clerk explained that the Board had to their credit in the Bank on current account £35 13a Sel, and on Loan ac- count £65 Sc 9d making a total of £lOl 2s sd. The him • diate liabilities of the Board amounted to £lO3 is 7d. Ho had closed the loan account and had made an affadavit that theaum had been properly spent in respect of the loan of £4675, and after the building of the school, and the payment of other expenses, there was the sum of £65 8s 9d, and be had received an order from the public Works Loan Commissioners to pay over that sum, to their credit in the Bank of England. If they drew out a cheque that evening to clear off the loan they would be left with a balance nf £35 13, gd to met liabilities ainvonting to £lO3 13 7d. If they allowed that matter to rem..ta over for another month until they got ' some mooey fr m the overseers they could do without ever- drawing their a, lount at the bsok.—lt was decided that a month should t.e allowed to elapse before they paid the money over to the Public Worts Loan Commissionere.—The Clerk stated that the estimated expenditure for the next six months amounted to £592 12s sd, and estimating £6O from school fees, and £l2O Government grants and other small items, the sum of £450 would, it appeared to him, meet all the requirements of the Board. There was a cer- tain elasticity in the Board Schools that he had not taken credit for, but there were also unexpected exnenses always cropping op.—Mr. Beckett thought they might anticipate a revenue of £2OO this year from the schools as the scholars were more numerous and more efficient. Besides half a years grant was lost last year. Ultimately it was reaelved to issue a precept upon the overseers for £450 to be paid on or before the 2nd May.

No sobjecf:can come before the people which will so I thoroughly arouse apprehension or awaken hope as those things which concern their physical well-being. If the bodily powers have gone, the value of life has departed, and anything which can avert such an end is not only of the greatest moment, but mast be within the highest mission of every well-conducted newspaper. Within the past year tt.e people in all parts of England have become more or less interested in the growing popularity of an important pro- duction. primarily designed for the good of mankind, and it was with a view to ascrtain definitely some facts connected therewith that a representative of this parer was comrois• sinned to investigate. What be learned can be gathered from the following:— _ .

o • Feeling that the chemists would be able to render valu- able information, our representative dropped in casually upon Mr, Alfred Raynor, of. No. 27, Chariot-street. He was well pleased at the object of the visit, and said that for a great length of time he had most seriously wondered why it was that diseases of the kidneys and liver, being so pro- valeta, were nct more succes fully treated by the physicians in general. He had frequently noticed that people affected with kidney or liter trouble would call upon him with the statement that they had been for a great length of time under the care of their physicians, but all to no purpose, and desiring him to recommend something, if he could, which would benefit them.

" A few months since," he:continued, " my attention was called to Warner's SAFE Cure, and I resolved to keep it in stock for the benefit of those troubled with the affections alluded to. Since I have kept it, I have been both pleased I and astonished to notice that cases of kidney and liver trouble which were really considered incurable, have com- pletely recovered by means of this remedy." From the testimony of this gentleman alone the incentive to gatherairther facts to corroborate the efficacy of this remedy was increased, and it wee with feelings of the most intense satisfaction that the investigator was enabled to personally interview a patient who had been taking the medicine. Mr. William Wavle!, of No 5, Paradise-place, Castle-street, a highly intelligent young engineer, whose statement can be thoroughly relied upon, felt only too glad of the opportunity to make known the details of his case and the benefit he has derived from the treatment. Said Mr. Wardel, " When I began the use of Warner's SAFE Cure ' I was a mere wrack, I had been unable to follow my business for months previously. I was in perpetual torment from the pain in my chest and back, a most distressing cough and profuse sweating at night, so that when morning came I was so exhausted that I was scarcely able to rise from my bed. I bad wasted away to almost a skeleton, and was most fearfully depressed both in mind and body, the more especially as my physican had told ray wife that it was utterly impossil-le for me to recover, and that she must prepare for the worst. When, at last, all hope had been abandoned, my attention was called to 'Warner's Saria Cure,' and although my means had become only too limited, I de- aired to try the medicine as a last resort. I have taken but a few bottles of the medicine, and I am already an entirely different man from the hopeless, despondent creature I was but a few short weeks ago." " Is it really possible, Mr. Wardel, that what you tell me is true? '

"What possible reason could I have," said he, "for deny- ing to a medicine that has done me so much good as this has the credit that is justly due to it, and to which I feel that I owe my life?" From information already received, the man of news then determined to see a Miss Thompson, of No. 2, Promenade Place, Vane-street, Spring Bank, whom he bad been told had been completply cured by the same medicine. Alias Thompson was only too willing to speak of her case. Said she:—

"For the space of twelve years I had been troubled with a most persistent and fearfully disfiguring redness of the face. So extensive was it, and 80 unsightly, that I had been forced to relinquish all srcietv, and to abstain from all those amusements of which young ladies are so fond."

"Bat could you obtain no relief at all ?" "No permanent or positive relief until quite recently. I must tell you that I had tried everything that I could think of, and that my friends would recommend, but all to no purpose. The doctor called the disease Acne, but could not seem to effect a cure. I was, at tact, almost hopeless of getting any better, when my attention was called to War- ner's SAFE remedies. Having tried so many different medi- cines without success. I must confess that my faith in this medicine was very, very slight. However. I began its use, and how great was my joy, as from day to day I watched anxiously the good effect, until at last I saw, with feelings that I cannot describe, that I was really cured." We next called upon Mrs Sarah Usher, of No. 25, Was- sand-street, Hessle-road. This lady stated that for a longl time she had been afflicted with lung difficulty, and had at one time been brought so low that her life was almost de- spaired of. She suffered constantly from a most distressing pain in the back, especially that portion just under the shoulder blades. She had a most wretched cough and al great difficulty of breathing. Her complexion, she told me, had teen pale,"and her general appearance that of a con- firmed invalid. Deprived, from the bad state of her nerves, of much-needed rest, her general strength had failed to such an extent that it was with the greatest difficulty she was able to perform even the very simplest house- hold duties. Mrs Usher informed our representative that, at last, she resorted to the use of Warner's Sara Care, as she became convinced that there was something wrong with her kidneys and liver, and the s.=.ciael has proved that her surmises were correct. She is a different person entirely, and has done work in the past week or two that she has been unable te perform before for years without most intense suffering. After congratulating this good lady upon the great im- provement in her condition, and with a mind busy with the indiepntable facts already g'eaned, we were enabled to inter- view Mrs Smedley, of Nia. 124, Adelaide-street. This lady stated that she had been a great martyr to liver trouble and nervous difficulty arising thPrefrom. "Year in and year out," said she, "the disease kept on gaining ground until my life was really a burden to roe. I had been under the treatment of our best physicians for a long time, but with- out avail."
"Did they afford you no relief ?". " Only temporary, but never what I could call positive relief."
"Do you consider that you are any better now ?" 'Unquestionably I am." "And to what do you attribute this change for the better 2"

"A gentleman in the Custom House, who had been tak- ing WARMER'S Sava Diabetes Crag, called my husband's attention to the WARNER'S SAFE CURE, and it was decided that I should try It. I have faithfully taken the medicine for only a very short space of time, and I am so much better that lam cenvinced my sufferings will soon end entirely. lean now go about my duties, formerly so irksome, with spirit and a sense of satisfaction and interest to which I have long been a stranger." Such statements from such sources are unquestionable, and conclusively prove the value of the remedy of which they speak. They are not from'obscure and unknown per- sons residing in distant parts of England, but of people liv- ing right here in Hull, where the truth of their assertions can be easily verified. Thousands are suffering to•day needlessly who might be made well and happy by the use of the same means tertified to shove. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CONFERENCE AT WALIIDEN.— The thirty-ninth annual conforence of the Primitive Methodist Ministerial Association—Manchester and Liver- pool districts—commenceu on Wednesday morning, in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Walkden, when there was a good attendance of ministers from Manchester, Liverpool, and other towns. The president, the Rev. J. Yearsley, of , Middleton, delivered the opening address on the influence Of the Church upon the national progress of the past fifty , years. Tarty the present is an age of economy. Although wages may have decreas.d, it it is certain that the work- ing man gets a corresponding benefit in the cheapness of articfes of daily consumption. Indeed, it is admitted on all Bides that a sovereign will go almost as far again as it would thirty years ago. The prices of sugar, tea, and food gene- rally, clearly demonstrate this; but perhaps the facilities for obtaining luxuries are equally important. The object ot one well-known firm, Messrs. W. Li A. Gilbey, is to edu- cate the people to consume wine and witer as a substitute for beer, much in the same manner as on the continent, and when one hears that they can sell not only Claret, but Port and SherrY. at Is. a bottle. their Lick does not appear diffi- cult. In France red wine is consumed by all the working classes, diluted with quite two-thirds water. Cases of drunkenness in wine producing countries are very rare, hence the subject is weriby of consideration even from a temperance point of Morning Post," April 6th, 1887.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held in the 1 Council Chamber of the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Aldermen Burgess, Harrison, Holmes, Chandley, Sutton, Webster; Councillors Brown, Jolley, Bolton, J. Pierpoint, Taylor, Dixon, F. A. Roberts, Dakin. H. Roberts, Litton. Grnenall, Ridir- way, Fleming, Tinsley, Hutchinson, Taylor, Wright, Francomb ; Messrs.. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), , Chorley (borough treasurer), Dr,Gornall (medical I officer),

div.head: WATCTI COMMITTEE.-A PROTBST.
div.p: WATCTI COMMITTEE.-A PROTBST.

This committees' minutes recommended the adoption of tenders for police clothing and equipments, and also recom- mended that Alderman Sutton and Councillor Litton be appointed members of the committee and Alderman Harri- son vice-chairman. The committee's estimate of expenditure for the year commencing 26th Mareb, 1887, mouated to a total of £2,278 19s. A further recommendation was that the tows crier be supplied with a suit of clothes. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman Hattnisolt seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor BOLTON called attention to the recommenda- tion of the committee that Alderman Sutton and Councillor Sutton be appointed members of the committee, and asked wby they bad dropped oat the name of Dr. Mackie. Had he resigned his position on the committee? For his (Councillor Boltop's) part he wished to be placed on that committee, and, in fact, he had a wish to be placed on some other committees; but becanee one or two aldermen thought ke was not a subject to be led by the nose he was not allowed to be on these committees. There were two members of the Council who were not on a single commit- tee; two were only on one committee, and he (Councillor Bolton) was one of the unfortunate three who were only on two Committees. They bad seven members on three com- mittees, eight ma four committees, four on five committees, two on six committees, and three or four on seven com- mittees, and one or two on eight committees. He thought there was an unequal division, and if this was the way in which the work of the Council was to be divided he should take good care, as far as he was concerned, to look very carefully at any resolutions that might be presented to the Council. Ile did not consider that one Alderman who had an idea that he should not be on a committee should say that he would oppose him. That Alderman was already on seven committees. A. councillor had also said that he would not sit on a single committee on which he was placed. There was hardly a committee of the Town Council that he was not debarred from.

The MAYOR, in reply t.) Councillor Bolton, said that the Ex- Mayor was a member ef the committee ex-officio. He might also draw attention to the fact that the committees were elected in November, which was the proper time to object to the names of certain gentlemen being placed en the com- mittee.

Councillor Dizorr thought that the work of the Council ought to be more equally divided. Mr. Roleen Heaton and Mr. Wright had applied two or three times in hie hearing to be placed on some committee, and there they had Mr. Frank Roberts with no office at all. The minutes were confirmed. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIMITING COMMITTEE.

This committee's minutes containe—d-;;;;II;;;;:-Ye.soln- tion, that the following plans ba approved: 11 houses in St. Mary's-street, La,chford, for Mr E Jameson (condition- ally); extensions to works in Thynne-street, for Mr Thomas Flvtcher (conditionally); 12 cottages in Battersby-lane, for Mr John Appleton; alterations and additions to mill at Bank Quay, for Messrs Litton and Co.; alterations and ad- ditions to shop in St. James'-street, Latchford, for MrJames Strange; 12 cottages in Thelwall-lane, for Mr E Rogers; ex- tension to Gospel Hall, off West-street, for Mr Thomas Brocklehnrst ; warehouse at Bank Quay Soapery, for Messrs Joseph Crosfield and Sons; 15 houses in Knutsford-road and Wash-lane, for Mrs M Dyson; six cottages in Norman- street, for Mr John Platt; two cottages in Latchford. for Mr IS It•eynolds ; shop in Bewsey-streat, for Mr Robert Heaton; alterations at house in Latchford, for Mr Joseph Hall; alterations to premises in Sankey-street, for Mr John Lythgoe.—Resolution, that a plot of land, containing 420 square yards or thereabouts, in St. Mary's-street, Latchford, I be purchased of Mr Edward Jameson, at the price of 7s fil per yard, for the purpose of widening the street to 36 feet, the plan of which improvement is now approved —The committee's estimate of expenditure for the ensuing year amounted to £3,310. Alderman Sca-roN moved, and Alderman Hartittsotc seconded, the confirmation of these minutes.

Councillor DIXON referred to the price paid for gas by that committee to the Gas Committee, and remarked that whilst everything else in Warrington had changed, the price charged the Street Improvement Committee for light- ing the lamps had not changed. The lamp near the Con- servative Club cost from £22 to £24 a year. lis should like to know when they were going to get the streets lighted for less money.

Alderman SuTrox said he supposed they were paying now for lighting the lamps what they had agreed to pay ac- cording to the understanding that bad been in existence for some time. The particular lamp referred to by Councillor Dixon was paid for according to meter.

The minetes were then confirmed. SANITAMY COMMITTEE.--RSTIMATED EXPENDTITIBB. The Sanitary Committee, which met on the 2nd March, recommended that the tender of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, for the supply of vitriol for 12 months at 303 per ton be accepted. The committee had resolved that in consequence of the prevalence of swine fever regulations should be made and put in force in the borough. The Medical officer (Dr. Gornall) presented the following re- port :—" I regret to say that there has been a serious exten- sion of measles during the last ten days. Since Monday, the 7th met, there have been over 100 notifications by medi- cal men. A more accurate state of affairs is arrived at by consulting the school registers, and I have obtained the fol- lowing information from the heads of the three schools where the disease is meet prevalent; St. Ann's School, boys, on the register, 257, absent 31; girls, 250,57; infants, 152, 52 ; St. Peter's, infants, 150, 38 ; Sliver-street, mixed, 220, 51; total, 1,029, 229. In any stage of a measles epidemic, personal communication is the principal method of exten- sion. This is promoted by children attending school in the early stage of the disease, which is frequently undistinguish- able, and by reterning to school before they cease to become infective. The only method at the present time of arresting its progress is by closing the schools in question, and I beg Ito recommend it. Amongst the many difficulties we have to contend with in coping witit an outbreak of meaeles is the tendency of teachers to induce parents to send their children back to school before the infective stage has passed. I know the Educational Departmsnt of the Local Government Board assures the teachers that absence from school from , epidemic disease will be allowed for in estimating the grant, but the teachers are loud in their complaints that when the examinations are held, this is lost sight of in valuing the standard of perfection expected from the schools."—lt was resolved that the town clerk write to the managers of the above schools, requesting them ta close the schools, in com- pliance with the recommendation of the medical officer.— The estimated expenditure of the committee for the ensuing Year amounted to £8,739 Bs, made up of the following items: Scavenging department, £2720 18s ; nightsoil, £3,011 5e ad ; Longford depot, £1,572 14s 6d ; intercepting depots department. £534 lOs ' • hospital department, £9OO. Alderman BURGESS moved, and Councillor H. ROBERTS seconded, the confirmation of these minutes. ' Councillor BOLTON said he observed that in the estimates for the ensuing year were nearly as much as those of last year. He thought they were to have a reduction in the rates all round owing to the very large profits that were be- ing made at Longford, and the success of the intercepting depots. He thought it was a had look-out when the com- mittee estimated to within about £2OO of last year's expen- diture. He should like to ask the chairman of the commit- tee when they might expect a reduction in the estimates, and whether all the money at Longford had been spent for nothing. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS said that they had beard glow- ing accoents of the saving of the Sanitary Committee, and he did anticipate that instead of an increase of the rates

they would have had a reduction. If it was correct, as he had been told, that a certain amount had to be paid out of revenue to meet capital expenditure, be should ask that the matter he put fairly before the Council with a view, if pos- sible, of capitalizing the amount, and of spreading the pay- ment over a number of years. He did not think that in these depressed times they ought to be saddled with the payment of any extra capital amount. (Hear, hear.) Councillor DixON said that he thought the expenditure would have been reduced. A number of gentlemen had spoken of the chairman of the committee in very flattering tones—he could never see the cause either—(laugbter)— and it seemed that he had only got to nut his hand up to be obeyed. (Laughter.) The estimates, he held, had increased every year. Only two months ago a gentleman rose in his plane and told them that the expenditure would be less by £1,500. Personally he bed a very strong notion of the works at Longford. He had christened them, in his own mind, a monument to the want of knowledge. (Laugh- ter.) Alderman MMUS Said that in comparing the estimates with those of last year, be found there was an actual reduc- tion of about £300; and there was included in the erimates a sum of a thousand pounds, which had been expended in excess of the estimated cost of the works. The estimated 'cost was £12,000, and they bad actually expended £13,000, and thmadditional £l,OOO would have to come out of the rate., Lastead of being paid out of borrowed money. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS wished to know whether it was not possible to capitalize the amount. Alderman HOLMES said they could only capitalize it by obtaining additional borrowing powers. COnlieillOr BOLTOY said that from what Aldermae Holmes, had stated it appcared that the Longford works next year would make a profit of over £1.300. He understood him to say that they were paying £l,OOO of the original one,- out of the rates, and making a reduction of a farther £3OO. He should like to have more light on the matter. Alderman StrroN : You should get your figures up, wan, Councillor BOLTON: lam afraid we are not furnished with figures. Councillor llENetv ROBERTS said if Mn. Bolton would refer to the minutes be would see that the sale of manure at Longford was estimated at £2,400. That sum was £BOO or 900 in excess of what was received dating the ptst year. The Sanitary Committee took credit that the ex. penditure would be £1,300 less than last year. Councillor F. A ROBERTS moved an amendment to the effect that that part of the minutes with regard to paying the £l,OOO out of the rates be referred back to the com- mittee.
THE EX
The MAYOSI thought the Sanitary Committee were wise in asking that the £l,OOO should be paid out of revenue, and he thought the town would benefit by it. . . . . . .

Alderman ButimEss in replying, said that for the informa- tion of Mr. F. A. Roberts and the rest of the Council, he might point oat what had been the expenditure for some Lime past which had the approval of the Council. In the year 1884-5 the expenditure was £9,876 lie; in 1885.6 it was £9,530; in 1886-7 it was £9,082 is; and according to, the estimates it would be next year £8,737 8, or £l,lOO less than it was four years ago. The MAYOR: That include the thousand? Alderman BURGESS, said it did, and he hoped, by econ- omy in every sense of the word their expenditure would be found to be something less than was estimated. He thought that the product at Longford might be expected to produce £1,300 or £1,400 more than last year, so that the prospect was not so bad as it would appear. He might remind Mr. Roberts that while they had been going through a period of ' great depression, the rates of the borough for the last year were 5s 8d in the £ against 6s 8d in 1881. He did not think they need distress thems,•lves much. He was sorry they had exceeded their estimates at Longford ; but an ex- cellent account could be given of the whole expenditure and how the excess was brought about. The Council had had no little to do with causing the increased exp3nditure by the votes given adversely to the interests of the borough and contrary to the desire of the committee. The minutes were then confirmed. Mr. Roberts' amend- ment not having been seconded.

MARKETS COMMITTEE. - THE MARKETS

div.head: QUESTION.
div.p: QUESTION.

The Markets Committee put forward an estimate of ex- penditure for the coming year of £1,176 14s. The total income from all sources during the past month was £240 7s 6,. Two memorials had been submitted to the commit- tee from persons describing themselves as dealers in eggs, butter, and cheese. One memorial, signed by 84 persons petitioned against removal of their stride from the new market shed to the old market shed; and the other, signed by 119 persons, was in favour of removal. The resolution passed by the committee was' that on reconsideration of the p• oposal to move the dealers in eggs butter, and cheese from the market shed into the market hail, it is not desirable to make any change in that direction for the present." Another memorial which had been presented to the committee was signed by 154 farmers of Warrington and district, and asked the committee to take into favourable consideratdin the proposed removal of the wholesale farm produce market from the fair ground to the north end of the covered shed.— This memorial, the committee decided, should be deferred for further consideration.—The memorial (the terms of which we have previously given), signed by 248 ratepayer, tradesmen, and property owners of the borough, had also been considered by the committee, who passed the following resolution upon it t—'6 That this committee, having received a numerously signed memorial from ratepayers and trades- men of Warrington relative to the management of the mar- ket, it is resolved that the committee do not at present see their way to make the alterations suggested as to stalls and other arrangements, and that a repert of their management be laid before the Council at its next meet- Alderman CITANDLEY said the committee had had var- ious memorials— four or five. The memorials first emanated from the butchers, requesting that the butter and egg people be removed back to the Market Hall. That was intended to have been done, but another memorial was re- ceived from the egg and butter dealers requesting that that action should not take place. Another memorial appeared requesting that they be taken back, and yet another memorial appeared from the farmers ',questing that pro- vision be made in the north end of the market for the potato market, and that the same be removed from the fair ground. Yet another memorial came from the Tradesmen and Pro. petty Owners' Association, complaining of the general arrangements and the management of the market. The memorial of the egg and butter people irst claimed atten- tion. There was a great deal of discussion on the subject as to whether it would be advisable to remove these people into the Market Hall. It was said with truth that it was inequitable to inconvenience one class of people who were content and were doing a good business, for the sake of bolstering up another class of people who were losing their business—at all events the butchers complained of the hard times sorely, and they proposed this as a panacea for their evils. The committede ultimately divided on this subject, with the result that they were equally divided as to opinion, and the casting vote was given by the Chairman. He should not detain them by bringing the arguments pro. and eon. With the diversity of opinion that there was on the subject, a portion of the committee felt that it was a serious thing to take any steps in .the

removal of - the seople to the Market Hall because it wettld be provocation of great cause of complaint amongst those left behind. The minutes simply asked for the thing to be postponed for future consideration. It would be unwise to rush into changes until every detail had been considered, and it was very probable that a further enlargement of the market would t Ake place: it was quite on the cards that they would have to open out the market into Queen-street. It was better to wait and see what the alterations would be. The memoridists complained that the markets had been devoted to the formation of a dry goods mirket. The complaint was unfounded, because there were now in the market a lees number of stalls than there had been for the last six years or so, so that it could scarcely be said that they had made increased provision for dry goods and hardware. It was also complained that the stalls were let at nominal rents, but the fact was that they were let at as high a rent as was allowed by the Board of Trade, and it was also a fact that the stafis were charged mere in proportion than the surrounding markets. With regard to the removal of the farmers from the fair ground to the covered market, they could not put the large number of traders who came with potatoes into the space at their disposal ; they would require double. With reference to this last mentioned memorial it represented about £l,OOO, the names attached to it numbering about 248.• They represen- ted one side of the question. There was a far larger num.

s rket..lo bay, and these people had a right to buy as cheaply as possible and to de. , mand that accommodation should be given to everyone so as to ensure the greatest competition, which would result to the advantage of the buyers. In the face of the memorial I be felt it his duty to send in his resignation as chairman of I the committee, and to plate his seat on the Market Corn- mittes at the disposal of the Cmncil, lest it might be con- sidered that he impregnated the committee with his views. He was not doing that in dudgeon, and was doing it before • the minutes were either confirmed or rejected, and so the action of the Council wonli not be said to have influenced him. The markets, he remarked, were in no way antago- nistic to the trade of the borough and brought a consider- number of people into the town. The increased facilities for travelling between Warrington and Manchester and Liverpool was some reason for depression in local trade. Councillor larrote seconded the confirmation of the minutes.

Cooacillor JOHN PIERPOINT proposed as an araendment "that the minutes of the Markets Committee be passed with the exception of the minute of the 21st March, 'that on reconsideration of the proposal to move the dealers in eggs, butter, and cheese from the Market Shed into the Mar- ket Hall, tt is not desirable to make any change in that di- rection at present." He moved his amendment, he said, with the greatest possible respect to the Markets Committee, and no One would be more sorry than he were Mr. Chandtey to resign his position as chairman of the committee. He pointed out that the committee were equally divided on the subject, that the Market Hall was a deserted place at pre- sent, and that since the butclwe were put there the amount received from rents had decreased from £640 per annum in 1881 to £lO3 in 1887. •

Councillor GRERNALL seconded the amendment. Councillor larrou said that the Committee were pretty agreed that there should be some farther arrangemente in the Market, and it was only recently that the committee bad a petition from the farmers to be removed from the fair ground, but they had not bad time to discuss it. Alderman SUTTON papported the amendment. He thought that the desire to increase the income of the Mar. ket, bad been the foremost one, and that the desire for the comfort and convenience of the public and the tenants was Only • secondary consideration.
Councillor &Was thought Councillor Pierpoint had made out a good case; he supported the amendment. Councillor FRA.NCOMB supported the amendment. . . .
Councillor BOLTON s ad he sboulci give his vote in favour of the amendment.

Councillor RIDGWAY supported the amendment and criti- cised the memorial against the removal of the egg and butter people to the Market Hall. Oat of the 84 signatures to that memorial he admitted that only three of them sold eggs, butter, and cheese, and they were, he believed, in marketolanguage termed hucksters. Councillor H. ROBERTS also supported the amendment, but at the Same time he thought be was expressing the opinion of the Council when be said he hoped Alderman Chandley would not think of retiring from his position as chairman Of the Markets Committee became of the adverse vote if there was one. (Hear, hear). Aldermaa WEBSTER defended the action of Alderman Chandley in giving the casting vote at the committee meet- ing, but said he would vote for the amendment. Alderman CHANDLEY, in replying, remarked that before the butchers began to make complaint of their trade going there had net been one complaint et any sort. As to the sensational complaints about butter melting—well, that was poetic. (Laughter). The amendment of Councillor .7 Pierpoint was then catried without opposition.

£24,809 19 11 £28232 4 0 Alderman Flotatas moved, and Councillor TINSLEY seconded, that the minutes be passed. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS was anxious that there should not be an increase in the rates this year. Some of the small ratepayers might not feel it as heavily as he did personally; but when they were suffdring from bad trade in Warrington, it seemed to him to lie a census matter to increase the rate by 4d in the pound. If it was possible for the Finance Com- mittee te tide over certain sums, and so equalise the pay- ments, they should do so, and give every assistance they could, Those miuutes were being passed, and an increase of 4cl in the rates was being sanctioned without any in- formation being given as to whether it was to be a per- manent advance or not. div.head: RATES.
div.p: THE RATES.

'Alderman HOLMES moved "That the Council estimate that the amount of £8,866 13s 2d will, in addition to the borough fund, be required and sufficient for the purposes to which the borough fund is applicable, under the Municipal Corporatioes Act, 1882, or otherwise by law, for the year to end 25th March, 1888. That the Council order a borough rate to be made in pursuance of the Munici- pal Corporations Act, 1882, in order to raise the said amount."

Alderman HoLstEs also moved "That an improvement rate of 3s in the £, to be collected by two half-yearly instal- ments, and a sewers rate of 4s in the b 3 laid." He an- nounced that the sewers rate was a little higher than that of last year, but this was owing to the surplus of the last rate being exhausted. Alderman Miasma seconded the first motion, and Councillor Tussmsr seconded the last named, and both were carried.

div.head: .THE TENDERS.
div.p: .THE TENDERS.

Councillor HENRY ROBERTS moved "that all the com- mittees of this Council shall be required for the future to procure the whole of their requirements whether for mate- tiara to be supplied or labour to be performed, or both, by tender, and that whenever the same shall involve the ex- penditure of £2O and upwards, tenders be publicly adver- tised for and that every accepted tender shall be published with the minutes of the committee connected therewith, together with the price and the name of the successful firm." He did not, he said, wish to cast any reflection on the officials of the Council ; but wai anxious that the responsi- bility Of ordering materials, and of giving orders for work to be done, should cease to rest in any degree upon the officials and be put upon the committees. (Hear, hear.) Atter the revelations they had read of during the last two or three days, he thought it was very essential that some alteration should be made in the direction he had proposed. Ile did not wish to impute anything to the officials of the Corporation, as he considered they had got the best officials any Corporation had. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON seconded the motion and said that he considered that 'everything should be pi:bile and above- board. He did not think they could do better than allow Councillors who were not members of the committees the opportunity of seeing what was done. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried. This was all the business before the Council.

An empty train passed over part of his limbs, both legs being broken, and one arm nearly cut off. His head was also fearfully injured. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

It is little wonder that the Speaker should have succumbed to the extraordinary pressure put upon him this session. What keeps the Speaker alive in average times is the alternation of duty with the Chairman of Committees. At this time of the year, in ordinary sessions,'the House of Commons should be in Committee on one or more of the prominent Bills in the Ministerial programme. The Chancellor of the Exchequer should have brought in the Bud- I get, and there would immediately follow weeks of I Committee of Supply. This is, of course, an • im- mense relief for the Speaker, though not quite to such an extent as appears from the Strangers' Gal- lery. When Committee is the business of the even- ing the Speaker leaves the chair as soon as ques- tions are over. But he may not leave the building. No one can say what a moment/may bring forth in, the House of Commons. An altercation may arise which must be immediately, reported to the Speaker; or the adjournment of the committee may be carried by a sudden and unexpected motion; or the Committee may be counted out, in any otwhich cases the Speaker must be brought in. Even if things go smoothly the unfortunate Speaker may not go to bed, however late the sitting may 'extend. When, the other week, the House at in Committee 01l night, the Speaker must needs have been throughout the long night ready to meet a sum- mons, which really did not come till one o'clock in the afternoon. To sit or lie half-dressed, momen- tarily expecting to hear the foot of the rushing 'messenger on the stairs, must be to a man of Mr. Peel's nervous temperament quite as bad, perhaps worse; than really sitting up. Another thing which has worried and depressed the Speaker, is the attack made upon him from cer- tain quarters of the House. These are unimportant, for no one would care what Mr. Conybeare, for ex- ample, says. .But they touch the highly sensitive nature of Mr. Peel, and lead him astray into emphatic refutation. It is absolutely true, as the Speaker said the other night, that he can afford to disregard the imputations upon his impartiality. The pity of it is that he does not do so. He openly writhes under attacks from the obscurist wasp in the House, and thereby invites fresh attacks. Men of the class who bring these wholly unfounded charges against him delight in nothing so much as to see his tall form drawn to its full height, his face pale with indignation, and his lips quivering with emotion. I often think Mr. Peel if he. had not been the Speaker, would have had a great suc- cess on the tragic stage. Nothing could have been more dramatic than his bearing on Monday night, when he Consumed Mr. Conybeare in his wrath. It was magnificent, but it was not business. If men of Mr. Conybeare's standing can thus cheaply move the Speaker to wrath, it is pretty certain that they will not deny themselves the pleasure of repeating the provecation. . .

Trio notable feature of the week in Parliament has been the sudden widening and deepening of the gulf that separates the Dissentients from the Liberal party. Dip to the very eve of the introduc- tion of the Coercion. Bill re-union was looked for. Many declined to believe that Mr. Chamberlain, and at least one-half of the Dissentient Liberals, would go the length of supporting a Tory Government in tightening the chains upon Ireland. The divisions which have taken place since the introduction of the Bill have definitively dispellid all hope of re- union. It is now war to the knife between the gaondam friends and colleagues. The hereditary animosity existing between Liberals and Conserva- tives is quite a mild passion as compared with that which exists between the Hartington-Cham- berlain party and the followers of Mr. Gladstone. The feeling in the House is, however, but a shadowy reflex of the passion that burns throughout the country. No one knows better than the Dissentient Liberals that whenever the General Election comes they will make a pretty holocaust. They notori- ously secured their seats on the last occasion by the aid of Tory votes. At the next contest the Tories will fight for their own band, and between the upper and nether millstone our respected friends will have a bad-time of it. This may be a satisfac- tory conclusion to those Liberals who thirst for vengeance. But its practical bearing on the posi- tion of to-day must not be lost sight of. The Dis- sentient Liberals, foreseeing their inevitable fate, are the more inclined to maintain their alliance with the Tories, and by keeping the Govern- ment in power to postpone dissolution. This is the real fcundation of the strength and security of the Government.. -

The Queen is now happily located at Aix, after a series of adventures which unpleasantly varied the usual monotony of a Royal journey. In the -first place Mr. Savil, the owner of the House where the Queen has been .stopping, at Cannes, was most un- fortunately and untimeously taken ill. It was not a passing attack of indisposition, but a serious ill- ness, which threatened to bring him to death's door. Of course the place is big enough for a bedroom to have been reserved for the sick man. But that ob- viously would not have been an agreeable incident in the holiday trip. Accordingly the unfortunate owner was removed to a neighbouring house, where, according to last accounts, he lies dangerously ill. Then the axle of the sleeping ear in which Her Majesty travelled got heated, and' threatened to break down. This is a matter of very common oc- currence on continental journeys. I know some people who recently visited the Riviera, and both going and coming were turned out of their beds in the middle of the night by an accident to the sleep- ing car. But Royalty is usually regarded as free from such vulgar accidents. Proof to the contrary will in one respect be welcomed by the railway authorities who have hitherto laboured under the suspicion of irate passengers, that the sleeping cars broke down to order, so that the trains might be redeemed of their heaviest burden: The Queen's visit to Cannes terminated last night, and she ar- rived at Aix-les-Bains to-day. This is a brief stay for the extraordinary prepara- tions involved in the trip. When the Queen travels on the Continent it is not an array of mere portmanteaux and boxes that suffice for the needs of the occasion. All the plate, china, and glass re- quired for the party are sent direct from Windsor Castle. A bed.ra not what Mr. Wemraick would have included in the category of "portable pro- perty." But the Queen's bed forms part of the lug- gage which accompanies her on the Continental trips. I believe there is nothing peculiar about the article. But for many years her Majesty has used one of a peculiar pattern, and believes she could not rest on any other. There is, accordingly, one at Balmoral, one at Windsor, one at Osborne, and a fourth for conveyance on chance journeys such as this to the Riviera.___ ' I

Mr. Herkomer withis year claim the full 1)1'1'6 - loge of aft E.A., and will show eight pictures on the line at the Royal Academy Exhibition. If merit is to be the test of support of such a claim no. one could dispute Mr. Herkomer's right. Ile has done an immense amount of work in the last twelve months, and all, save perhaps a landscape, is excel- lent. Lookinground his well filled studio, at a private view the other day, I asked in amazement whether he had done all these since the last exhibi- tion. He told me that what was being shown was only a portion of his year's work, which included not less than thirty-four complete pictures. At Mr. Herkomer's prices this must reptesent a pretty good income. But he does not sell all his works. What is perhaps the gem of his collection will not come Upon the market, though it will be ex- hibited at the Academy. It is the portrait of a lady in black, a companion picture to the lady in white, which formed a striking feature in last year's show. This is a beginning of types of beauty which Mr. Herkomer keeps for himself. It is, he says, a way he has of insuring his life. Instead of paying large yearly preMiums he paints a picture

or two, hangs them on his own walls, and feels ihat in case of anything happening to him his family will be well provided for. Among his portraits of this year is a capital one of Henry Stanley. Others , are Mr. Burnand, Sir Edward Watkin, and Mr. Sid- ney Buxton. These are all good. But a singular , interest hangs over a wonderful portrait ()Qin Faw- cett. This is strikingly lifelike, and yet Mr. ' Herkomer saw Mr. Fawcett only once. He has begun and finished the portrait since the death of the original. 1 Mrs. Brown Potter is quietly simmering out at the Haymarket. The injudicious adulation of some elderly friends was enough to forestall her ruin: It created something of a prejudice against her,which would take greater talents than hers to overcome. i There is a pretty story going about which is about the best thing I have heard in relation to her. It is said that when she visited Ireland the Custom , House officers, beginning to examine her baggage, asked if she had any arms in her trunk. "No," she said, "but I have two arms on my trunk, and I have come to embrace all Ireland with them, God bless her !" But was Mrs. Brown Potter ever in Ireland.

UGBY RULES. Sr. PAUL'S CHOIR V. BEWSEY WHITE STAR.—Played on the ground of the latter and resulted in a draw in favour of the choir. St. Paul's Choir, 1 goal, 4 minors; Star, 1 goal, 2 minors.

BEWSEY ROVERS V. WARRINGTON WANDERERS.—A match was played between the above clubs on the ground of the latter, and resulted in an easy victory for the Rovers by two goals, two tries, and four minors to two minors. WARRINGTON Sr. PAUL'S V. SUTTON—This match was played at Warringtoi, on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the home team, after a very good game, by one goal, four tries, and six minors to one minor. The tries were obtained by McCue (3), Lally, and Oxley. WIDNES V. Sr. HELENS—This hastily-arranged match ' was played at Widnes, on Tuesday. Neither team was fully represented, the visitors being weak at bock. Two "thirties" were played, and in the first half Slevin, who was playing 1 for St. Helens, put In some good runs, but the home team I paid him too much attention. Plumoton, for Widnes, put in some good kicks, and Smith, Kiddie, Borthwick. and Leatherbarrow showed up well for their respective sides, in the dribbling department. Five minora were credited to i the home team at halftime. On change of ends Widnes assumed the aggressive, and had pretty much the hest of ! the game, Hardman, and Parkinson being credited with tries, and Plumpton converted them both into the , premier point. The St. Helens men made one or two 1 good rushes, and looked on one occasion like scoring, but 1 a good chance was missed, and Widnes touched down, a 1 proceeding which they had to repeat later on, these being ! the only points scored by the visitors. The game terminated ' in a win for Widnes by two goals and eight minors to two minors. WARRINGTON " A " TRAM V. SOUTHPORT OLYMPLO IST. —The Warrington " A " team had a most enjoyable journey to Southport on Saturday to play the Southport Olympic Ist team. They only took a weak team, being short of their usual half backs and several forwards. Slack kicked off for Southport, the ball going into touch in goal. Jolley dropped out, a scrimmage being formed in centre. The Warrington forwards, headed by Adamson, Molvneaux, and Thornier. broke away, and some good passing between Jones, Belshaw, aud Nevins ensued, the latter player kick- ing a dead ball. Slack dropped out, and Hackett returned. The home forwards then went away with a dribble, which Jones stopped. Summers and Toole made a rush with the ball, but Jolley returned nicely into touch. Lund next put in a capital run, Adamson bringing him down. J Smith next obtained a free kick, Hackett col- laring Summers before he could return. Jones gave Boardman a good pass, this player kicking down the field. Moorfield got hold, bat was soon stopped by Belehaw, but be again obtained possession and put in a splendid run, Smith pushing him into touch. Ashurst, Eyes, Bate, and Adamson cleared their lines with a grand dribble, taking play to the home 25, but Woodworth re- moved to centre. Hackett now got in a good pass to Bel- show, who failed to score, Rimmer relieving the pressure by a good kick. Rimmer got nessession and kicked to Board- man, who made a capital run in but failed to improve the point. Slack dropped out, and no return being made a scrimmage was formed in centre. Adamson, Ashurst, Moly- neaux, and Lloyd dribbled to the home line, where Rimmer intercepted a pass and took play to centre. Moorfield next put In a splendid run, passing all but Jolley, who brought him down finely. Jones here passed to Boardman, who kicked into touch. Half time was called shortly afterwards, the score being Warrington one try and one minor to one minor. Ashurst re-started, and Moorfield returned into touch. Hackett passed nicely to Nevins, who dropped at goal, a minor resulting. Jtilley returned the drop out into touch, and Hackett and Adamson were next con- spicuous with a good dribble to the line, South- port haring to concede a minor. After the drop out Bel- shaw passed to Board, who put in a good kick, Ashurst collaring Robinson before he could part with the ball. The home forwards broke away, and Lund getting hold not in a nice run, being pushed into touch by Jolley. Nevins now kicked well up the field, Robinson being again collared with the ball by Adamson. Barnes here got possession, and gained a splendid try, no god re- sulting. The Southport men again pressed their opponents, Jolley being forced to save. Shortly after the drop out Suitmers passed forward to Lund, who ran in behind the Posts, hut the try was disputed by the vibitors, and South. port kicked at goal under protest, no goal resulting. Ashurst dropped out, and Adamson following up prevented Barnes frcm returning. The Warrington forwards then worked the ball neat the home line, where play was located when time was called, the .game ending in a draw—South- port one try, one disputed try, and three minors to Warring- ton one try and three minor points. Teams :—Warrington ; Full hack, Jolley • thre—quarter backs, Boardman, Belshaw, and Nevins • haff-backs, Jones and Hackett; forwards, Molyneaux:Adamson, Eyes, Thornier, Coyne, Lloyd, Bate, Smith, and Ashurst Southport Olympic: Full back, Robinson ; three-quarter backs, Barnes, Lund, and Moor- field ; half backs, Summers and Rimmer • forwards, Slack (captain), Parry, Rickerby, Fletcher, Webster, Woodworth, Toole, Marshall, and Jones.

, RUNCORN V. RIECLES.—Firie weather favoured the meet- ing of these clubs, on the ground of the former on Saturday, and a large attendance of spectators assembled to witness the game, which, however, was an uninteresting one, the. visitors being defeated by three goals, three tries, and nine minors to nil. Ectles won the toss, and W Hughes started the leather for Runcorn, who played with the wind and sub against them. The kick off was followed tip and scrimmaged in the visitors' quarters, and from a line out Worthington removed play to midfield, where the leather was located for some time. W Hughes and Broady were the first to shift the scene, the last-named dribbling well. Halsall soon ran the leather back, but was replied to by Cawley. Nunn here got in some good foot play for Eccles, and was near scoring when he fell into the hands of Woods, though Andrews was left to return the leather to neutral ground, where it was confined for some time ; but some rapid passes and exchanges freely indulged in by ooth sides gave Eccles a temporary advantage, the ball settling down for a while in Runcorn territory. It Hughes eventually changed the venue to the half flag, and Speakman continued the play into Eccles' quarters, where he threw to Davies on the right, who reached his opponents' 25. The play was still very fast, the ball visiting either, end rapidly. After the Eccles for- wards had got in a good dribble, Andrews and H Hughes re- spectively led the home team on the visitors' lines, where the back was broken up. Worthington punting to midfield, the forwards further improved their position, and the ball went into touch in the home 25. Give-and-take play con- tinued for some time, but of a very uninterestibg character, till Wright ran into his opponents' quarters, and, Halsall having missed his kick, Gatley, taking the ball on the bounce, rushed it over and grounded. Eccles unsuccessfully appealed against the point, and Broady failed to improve upon it. 'The drop out mr.s run back by Wainwright, who reached the visitors' 25 before he was stopped. H. Hughes was baulked, Speakman immediately after kicking the ball dead. The drop oat was followed up by Worthington. whose punt fell into Woods' hands, and he ran it out to the 25, whence it was rushed into Eccles territory, where some fine passing by Runcorn was shown—Broady to Andrews, the latter to Davies, who transferred back to Andrews, and the last-named finished off the sequencowith a try—another failure at goal by Broady. At half-time the score was two tries and a minor in favour of Runcorn. The home team now had the sun in their favour. Nunn restarted the lea- ther, which was packed in the centre, where play for a time followed, but the Cheshire men soon asserted their super- iority, and a great change came over the play of both teams, the ball now being rarely outside the vieitors' 25. Eccles had to touchdown twice in rapid succession, and then Indrews wak. prominent with a pass to Speakman, who on being tackled kicked forward, and Wainwright bounded over, Faulkner b3ing no more successful at place than Broady. Wright next brought the leather back and passed to H. Hughes who in front of the poets droppeg a good goal. For a few minutes Eccles tried to exert themselves, and made a short raid in Runcorn ground, which Davies, however, easily shifted, and Wright, taking up the play, got over, but more disputing on the part of the visitors resulted ire the referee disallowing the point. Speakman, however, had revenge by dropping a second goal in a short time afterwards, and H Hughes secured the next try, some good passing by Davies, Broady, and Lewis having led up to it, Woods placing an easy goal from the front of the posts The efforts of the Eccles team were now useless, and minors were rapidly noted. Davies also scored another try, which was again disallowed, and time was called without any additional point being scored, Runcorn winning as above. The losers were best represented forward, where some good open work was frequently naticed, but their backs were of little use, their play being a trifle inclined to roughness. Runcorn exhibited their usual combination, but the sun

shining brightly in their faces in the first bale marred their , Play. Teams ;—Runcorn : T. Wood., back; T. Davite?' H. C. Speakman, and H. Cawley, three-quarter backs l; Hughes and H.
