RETURN WAlrrsn.—Of the "burning questions" that end in smoke. Miss Blank, to her cousin, who has inadvertently ad- mired her foot; "Yes, papa thinks so much of my foot that while we were in Italy he tried his best to persuade me to have a bust made of it." The progress of the domestic servant has been thug• defined:--First week—" Treasure.' Second—".l must say that Ann is careless." Third—" My very best China, too." Fourth—" You will pack your things and go now." •

Pretty servant-girl, who has been taken half a mile beyond her destination—" It's really too bad ; I told you when I first gbt in where I wished to be set down." 'Bus conductor—" Well, miss, I let you get out as soon as ever I could find it in my 'art to part with you." A fat woman entered a crowded street-car and, seizing a strap, stood on a gentleman's toes. As soon as he could extricate himself he arose and offered her his seat. "You are very kind, sir," she said. "Not at all, madam," he replied, "it s not kindness, it's self- defence." Miss V.—" You seem to be the best man at all the weddings, Mr. B. When are you going to take a leading part yourself ? " Mr. B.—" Oh, there are as good fish in the sea as ever came out of it ?" 'Miss V.— "Yes; but don't you think the bait is getting a little stale ?" HE DIDN'T Rmi.—Moses Case was an albino, whiter than a Caucasian, though his parents were pure blacks. He went to the Mexican war as a musician in a Ken-

tucky regiment. Efe—waTtiiipp—ose—d to have made a precipitate retreat On one occasion, and, on being asked if he did not run, replied: Not exactly, but if I.had been gob' for a doctor you would have thought the man was very sick." LATEST Tcsr.—Wife, with head out of second-storey window "Is that you, John Smith ?" Husband at front-door: Yfth, m'dear." . Wife : "Well, say, Chrysanthemum,' or you don't get into this house to- night." Husband, heroically: Ch-chran-sythe-mum, m'clear." Wife, banging the window: "Good night." Two old men, lamenting the changes which have taken place. First old man (sadly) : "I cannot enjoy myself now as I could when I was a boy. I can't eat had as much." Second old man: "I cannot eat as much now as I could wh&l I was a boy, but I regard that as rather a wise provision." "Why so ?" " l3ecause I haven't half as much to eat."
_ Lord Beaconsfield received a deputation once of which . .

the late Charles Reade was a member. When Reade rose to speak, his lordship said, "Pray be seated, Mr. Reade." "I would rather stand, my lord," was the reply; "I can make a longer speech when standing than I can when sitting." "I am very sorry to hear it," was the Premier's comment.

"It's a solemn thing, young man," said the broken- hearted father, "to come into the home of an old man and take away his only daughter, the light of the house- hold, and the prop and solace of his declining years. But you have my blessing, and I wish you every joy and—" "But I won't take her away, sir," interrupted the young man, inexpressibly affected. "We'll both stay with you." A DOLL Boy.—" Thomas, you have disobeyed your grandfather." "No I didn't, ma." "Yes you did. Have you not been in swimming ?" "Yes, ma." "Didn't I hear him say to you not to go in swimming ?" "Oh, he didn't tell us that; he only came out and said: Boys, I wouldn't go in swimming,' and I shouldn't think he would, an old rheumaticky man like him; but he didn't say nothin' about our going in swimming." "Hello, Sam," said a gentleman to an old negro riding along on an old mule, "where did you get that beast ?" "I buyed 'im in cou'se ; yo' didn't tink I stoled 'im, did yo' ?" "I wasn't sure. -What did you give for him ?" "I gib my note, ash, for fawty dollahs !" "Your note, Sam ?" In cau'se, ash !" "Why, you'll never pay it." " Cou'se I won't, boss. Yo' don't recon dat man specs Pse gwine to pay for dat mule, an' pay for dat note, besides, does yo? No, sah, hit's as much as dis darkey kin do to pay fo' de mule." SHALL WE CALL Imo Womui ?—" James," said a Pitts- burgh grocer to his clerk, "you mustn't say 'lady' to the women customers any more; they don't like the term." •• All right, sir," replied James; and presently Mrs. Wayback came in. "I want a Philadelphia dry picked codfish," she said, "and three bars of soap.' "Yes, woman," responded James; "where'll you have 'ern sent ?" "Don't you 'woman' me, you young snap- perhead," said Mrs. Wayback, eyeing him with disfavour. "I'm a lady, an' don't you forget it," and she flounced out.

A certain. American judge was advocating capital punishment. An Irishman who was present had listened for some time to the discussion, vainly trying to get in a word; at last he succeeded, and the following dialogue took place between him and the judge. "So yez wud hang a man for killing another won, wud ye?' "That is my way, sir." " Wud yea hang him for the furst won he kilt, yer honour?" "If it was clearly proved that he had killed a man, certainly." "Oh, that wud not do at all, at all! Hanging a man is purty hard on him." "So I suppose." "An' if ye hanged a man for killing the furst won, what wud yea do with him for the sicond offinse• , • .

_ A New Englander, who was a wag, kept an eating- house near Boston, where, as he used to say, you could get anything that was ever made to eat. One day in came a New Yorker, and, stepping up to the bar, asked the landlord what he could give him for his dinner. "Anything, sir," said the host, "anything from a pickled elephant to a canary bird's tongue." "Waal," said the New Yorker, eyeing him, "I guess I'll take a piece of pickled elephant." "Well, we've got 'em—got em all ready, right here in the house; but you'll have to take a whole 'un, 'cause we never cut 'em' The New Yorker thought he would take some codfish and potatoes: EASY WAY TO SECURE SHORT SERMONS.—The 'late Archbishop Trench had a keen sense of fun. While he was Dean of Westminster it became the turn of Canon Cureton to preach at the Abbey on a certain saint's day. On such days the boys of Westminster School attended service, and after service had the rest of the day as a holiday. While Mr. Cureton, on the morning of the day when he was to officiate, was looking over his sermon at the breakfast-table, his son asked, in a voice vibrating with anxiety, "Father, is yours a long sermon to-day?" "No, Jimmy, not very." "But how long? Please tell me." "Well, about twoty minutes, I should say. But why are you so anxious to know ?" "Because, father, the boys say they will thrash me awfully if you are more than half-an-hour." After the service was over, Mr. Cureton told Dean Trench the story. " Dear, dear," he replied, what a pity Words- worth has no sons in the school !" Canon Wordsworth used to preach sermons an hour, and sometimes an hour and a-half, in length.

div.p: PIMLIC-HOUSE RANSACKED Al' ST.
HELENS. EXTRAORDINARY CONFESSIONS.

An extraordinary charge of house-breaking, in which revelations of an exceptional character were Ilmade, was investigated at the Town Hall, on Satur- day forenoon, before Alderman J. Harrison. John Fairclough and his son John (11 years old), of 9, Havelock- street; Richard Willett (13), of Raven-street ; William Henry Holmes (11), of Shaw-street, and William Woods, a young man residing in Raven-street, were charged with breaking and entering into the Salisbury Hotel, and stealing a large quantity of miscellaneous articles, the property of John Ormerod, of Manchester, owner of the hotel. The 'prosecution was conducted by Mr. R.W. H. Thomas, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended the prisoners. Mr. Thomas briefly stated the circumstances to the effect that the place was at present untenanted, but was left secure on Saturday, the 19th ult. On the following Monday .right it was discovered to have been broken into, and a large quantity of household goods were missing. He asked in order that justice might be secured that the prisoner Holmes might be discharged, so that he might be called as a witacss.—The prisoner Holmes was then discharged, and Mr. Thomas asked for the other prisoners to be committed for trial.

Henry Finch, licensed victualler at present residing at the Abbey Lakes Hotel, near Wigan. said he was formerly tenant of the Salisbury Hotel. On the Saturday previous, he left the place safe and locked up, but when he visited it on the following Tuesday morning be found the back gates open and a back window, including a portion of the frame, had been broken. On entering he found that the place had been much upset. Things had been thrown from upstairs down to the bottom, while a lot of articles were missing. Among the articles he missed were glass and pewter measures, flock beds, crockery, &c., which were the property of the owner of the public hence, Mr. John °ramrod, publican, of M an- chester. In reply to Mr. Swift witness said he could not per- sotnlly identify any ef the articles. _ . .

Mrs-. Finch, 'wife-of the last witness, said she had found the Salisbury Hotel had been entered and a number of arti- cles taken away. She missed a dozen brass hooks, 6 Cups and saucers, 12 plates, 1 kettle, 2 fenders, 0 tin canisters, 6 knifes, 6 forks, some dishes and pint mugs, four spittoons, four stools, one set of pewter measures, some bottles of mineral water, a bottle containing a wooden cross, some email top glasses, two pictures, half dozen tea spoons, two flock beds, two blankets, one bolster, 3 chairs, one table, 3 window blinds, one quilt, two brooms, and two pair of dumbbells. The total value of the goods was about £4. Several of the articles produced were similar to those in use at the Salisbury Hotel. William Henry Holmes, the discharged prisoner, said he was 11 years of age, and lived at 20 Shaw-street. On Satur- day afternoon he was with Richard Willets and yeung John Fairclough. They went to the Z:ababury Hotel, and went in- to the back yard through the door, which was open. The witness continued his evidence as follows :—We broke a window and got inside. Willetts went in first, then Fair. dough, an 4 then me. I took acan full of pine apple syrup, and Willetts took some knives and forks. We then went into the bar and took some cider. We then went out, and we went again about half-past nine the same night, when the prisoner Woods joined us and went with us. We again went inside the Salisbury. Willetts opened the door and admitted Woods, who "tapped " a barrel of porter and drew it into a to gillon bottle, Us also took a small keg

of beer, which I carried home for him. He also took a chisel, a hammer, a pepper bottle, and a match stand. Willetts took some cups and saucers; and Woods also took a teapot, which he gave to, little Fairclough. All these goods were taken to our house. We did not, go again that night, but we again went on Sanday afternoon. Willetts, I, and young Fairclough, went together, and we:each took two bottles of mineral water, which we took into the loft and drank the, mineral water. On Sunday morning Woods and Mr. Fairclough came to our house and stayed about three- quarters of an hour. Woods, Mr. Fairclough, and Winans then went away, but Came back again. Woods had a quart of porter, Willetts had a satchel full of mineral waters, and Fairclough had some brass i3alls, which were put in the satcbell. Willetts else gave Fairclough some knives and Wei. Myself and Willetts drank some cider, and Woods and Fairclough had some porter. While we were drinking Fairclough said be would murder his son if he told anything about it. —John Fairclough junior, here shouted from 'the dock: "He never said anything to me, you lying beggar." —ln reply to Mr. Swift, witness added that Willetts told Woods on Saturday that. there was some "cheap beer " at the Salisbury Hotel. Woods had had some drink. The boy Fairclongh was away from home all Saturday night, and stayed at witness'a house. On Sunday morning his father came looking for him, and on finding him at witness's home his father sent him home. Elizabeth Graham. mother otthe last witness, stated that the prisoner Woods came to her house about eleven o'clock on Saturday night carrying a small bottle on his shoulder. He asked witness to have a drink and she drank some porter. Mrs. Woods was there as well. On the next morning wit- ness found a keg of beer in her back yard. P.C. Clarkson then gave evidence as to the apprehension of the prisoners, and said he charged them with the offence. In reply John Fairclough,. jun. said Holmes broke the window and then, broke a glass pane and went upstairs and took two blankets with red stripes on, and his mother tore them off and put them in the. fire. He told his mother where he had got them from, saying the Sails. bury Hotel. He also took a big bottle of porter, and a small keg of ale and gave them to his mother. He took some curtains and some mugs and gave them to his mother, and she told him to go again, and said' You can go in and Bill Woods can keep watch.' He went again and got some red etriped blinds, which are at Willett's, and carried and gave them to Nellie Woods. Richard Willets took four soda water bottles, about ten bottles of pop, and ,two bogies of ale, and he took them home, and Bill Woods and Nelly supped ahem. • He carried them in a basket belonging to Wales's. I was with,Willets when the policeman stopped him on Saturday night, carrying the bottles, and Bill Woods was thereqind he ran away yrith a chair which lie had taken from the Salisbury Hotel. Holmes lifted me up, and I went through the window and took two red striped blind and gave them to Nelly Woods." The prisoner Holmes said "I took a few bottles of cider and lemonade, and two bottles of &Oa water, end carried a keg of beer for Bill Woods, who came into the hotel with a lamp, and asked me to carry the keg ter him.. I . took a blanket and left it on the counter in the bar. and Dick Willets took it. I left one in the cellar, which he bad taken himself. I took the bottles home and Bill Woods drank some. I drank two bottles of lemonade and a bottle of cider; and my mother drank some stout from a big bottle which Bill Woods carried. I took about six cups, six saucers, and five plates, and my mother put them in the pantry." • - - Richard Willets said : " Helmei took about four glasses and some cider, and about sin large plates and some cups and saucers, and Bill Woods gave 'them to his mother, and put them in the pantry. She asked .Ifolmes where he got them and he said, the Salisbury Hotel. • Bill Woods took abeut twelve brass nails off a shelf, a chisel, and a big barn- mer and went into the cellar and tapped a barrel of stout, and drank some and got drunk, and also drank from a barrel of beer. • He also took some tea' cups, two kettles, and fen- ders, and bedsteads. Bill Woods and John Fairclough went both ots Saturday night and Sunday night. John Fairclough took some pots and glassps, and drank some stout out of a barrel, and took a bottle of lemonade." John Fairclough the elder replied as follows :—"I was looking for my boy on Sunday morning, and I saw Dick Willetts at the end of Shaw-street. He told me where my boy was, and alsO said: "I know where there is some cheap ale.' I asked him where it was, and he said, 'The Salisbury Hotel.' I and Bill Woods and Helmets and Dick Woods found the yard gate open and orse of the windows broken, and the back door was open, and we aU wen‘ into the cellar and had two pints of porter each out of a barrel and mixed it with ginger beer, and we came out and I never went down afterwards." William Woods said: "What Falrelough has said is time., I took no more than the porter." P.C. fame deposed tw having searched Willet's house (where the prisoner Woods also lived), and' found the cigar boxes produced, containing the glasses produced. Edward Swift, a labourer, 71, Morley-street, said he was going to his Work on Wedneaday morning, when be found the winciew Wads and curtains and picture frames produced on some waste laud near Bath-street. He gave them to the police. Mr. Swift addressed the Bench at considerable length on behalf of the prisoners, and said it was quite cleat that the skier Fairolough had only gone to the place' on one occasion, and then it bad been broken into. The elder Fairclough and the prisoner Woods had both had some drink on the Saturday night, and he (Mr. Swift) did not think the charge against them was of a serious nature. He asked the Bench to reduce the charge to one of stealing and deal with the case without committing the prisoners for trial. The Bench said it appeared that the elder Fairclough had been in prison since the preceding Tuesday, and as his offence seemed, to be very light he would be discharged. The other three prisoners would be committed for trial.— Mr. Swift applied for the prisoners to be admitted to ball, and the lads were admitted to bail in one sprety of £5 each, while in Woods' case the bail was fixed at himself'dn £2O and two sureties of £lO each.

- - - - THE OVERSEERS OF FRODSHAM LORDSHIP. Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last I see there is a "Touch and go" on the nomination of overseers for Frod- sham Lordship, which, t think, gives a wrong impression to your readers. Not living at Frodsham Lordship, I have no voice in the matter, but I happened to be at the Eddisbary Petty Sessions and beard the case when it was brought up before the magistrates, and I think the statemeet as made in your paper unfair to Lord Tollemache, who was guided, I believe, by the other magistrates, and chiefly by Mr. Iligson, who knows the place well, and also the inhabitaats of the lordship. As stated in your paper, Mr. Hargreaves was nominated at a ratepayers' meeting by about two votes to one, but allow me to say. sir, "that meeting" was a packed meeting, held at a public-house. I believe it was the pints of beer, &c, that got his voters together. If a poll of the voters had been taken instead of a show of hands counted. Mr. Hargreaves would have been where he is now, "not in it." His supporters were mostly cot- tagers with one vote. whereas Mr. Percival's supporters in more cases than one were able to give 4,5, and 6 votes each. I may also say that Mr. Percival has lived in the Lordship 20 years, and has been overseer for 7 years. He is well-known and highly respected as a thorough conscientious mar, a state- ment which was well borne out by a petition read before Lord Tollemache and the other magistrates. Mr. Percival is, too, rated on over £2OO per year, while Mr. Hargreaves is only rated on about £l4 or £l9 per year. In conclusion I may say this is not the first attempt Mr. Hargreaves has made to get into office. I hope he will profit by his lessons.—l emain, yours, &c., FAIR PLAY. Frodsham, April 6th, 1887. tour point is—and we still maintain it—that if the rate- payers are called together for township business their decision should be respected. We do not believe in guag- ing men either by their titles or their money bags.— En. Ex.] LORD SELBORNE AND THE IRISH PRIESTHOOD. Sir.—Lord Selborne seetllll to be in great trouble lest the ten commandments should all come to grief through the action now being taken by the Irish priesthood. I suppose his Lordship will allow that, to have full effect, the com- mandments should be binding all round. They were surely never given to enforce a law which, in the words of General Boller, hes hitherto " been all on one side." His lordship cites the 6th commandment, and I suppose in doing so would have us accept it as a reason why he supports his natural allies, the Tories. As a matter of fact Ireland is free of crime as compared with England, and we have the reports of Judges during their recent circuits in proof of this. What crime she has is of a purely agrarian character. But when his lordship goes further and insists that the Bth and 10th commandments are being broken, it is time we asked for proof. Thou shalt not steal." Let us see who has been stealing., and who is the thief. Colonel Loftus Tottenham, Ml'., is a representative Irish landlord, and a sample of how he deals with his tenants will aid US in this. The Land Commissioaers sitting at 'Mena Hamilton. had before them the cases of five tenants of this model landlord. The following table is the result Old rent New rent Percentage 2 sa 2 9 d reduction, Owen Rooney 8 0 0 315 0 _ 53 Denis Rooney 7 8 6 115 0 49 John Rooney 612 0 30 0 56 Midget 'Kenny 17 17 6 6 10 0 65 M. McChristin 47 10 0 20 0 0 58

Percentage of old rack rent over judicial rent one hundred and thirty six per cent. NOW, air, who has been stealing here? And why should the ten commandments be hurled at the poor tenant's bead ? Lord Selborne knew of their existences some years ago. Why did he not give the land- lords the benefit of his knowledge? His Lordship says the priesthood are now calling "evil good and good evil ;" and, along with his so-called Liberal Unionist friends, deplores that the Church of Rome should "ally itself anywhere with the forces of anarchy and dis- order." Just so, the priesthood should have allied itself with law and order. or in other words, it should have sided with those who would keep Ireland in the state so well described by Sir Robert Peel in June, in 1847. Famine is in thy cheek Need and oppression starveth in thine eyes; Upon thy back hangs ragged misery; The world is not thy Mead. nor the world's law. The world affords no law to make thee riek ;

Then be not poor, but break it. Allow me to cite an authority, perhaps not SO high as Lord Selborne's' yet his lordship is proud of his company; I refer to John Bright, and the quotations I give effectually answer all cavillers against the present action of the Catholic priesthood, and against the American Irish But some say (and this is not an ancommcn thingl—SOMe say that the priests of the popular Church in Ireland have been the cause of much discontent, I believe there is no class of man in Ireland who have a deeper interest in a prosperous and numerous community than the priests of the Catholic Church; and further, I believe that no men have suffered more—have suffered more, I mean, in mind and in feeling—from witnessing the miseries and the desolation which during the last century (to go no further back) have stricken and afflicted the Irish people,"—Speech at Dublin, October 30, 1866. Again :—" You may depend anon it that if the Irish in America, haying left this country, settle there with so strong an hostility to us, they have had their reasons; and if, being there. with that feelin.: of affection for their native country which in all other cases in which we are not concerned we admire and ebverence, they interfere in Ireland, and stir up there the sedition that now exisits, depend upon it there is in the condition of Ireland a state of things which greatly favours their attempts. There can be no continued fire without fuel."—Speech in the House of Commons, Feb. 17,
1866. Those so-called Unionists who wculd goad the Irish to rebellion, and who now support a Coercion Gag in order to gain a Coercion Bill will do well to ponder the above quo- tations. UNIONIST.

THE GOVERNMENTsOF IRELAND. Sir,—ln your issue of the 4th inst., I felt somewhat grati- fied when I perused your correspondence column, to find space for a Unionist putting in a plea for Ireland. But I soon found out that your correspondent, who signs himself "Unionist," was no Unionist at all, and merely used the term, perhaps, to attract the attention of the real Unionists, who have, according to his opinion, been drawn into a tales position. Well, it Is very' kind of your correspondent to moan and wail for us, and to pray for us to consider, ereit be too late, whither we are being hurried. I can assure him that the Unionists have considered their position, and most bitterly lament the false position which Mr. Gladstone has brought , himself and the country to by his unwise scheme which he a has mistakenly termed "a bill for the better government of Ireland." The Liberal Unionists are perfectly aware that , they have in the past had to differ very largely with the principles of the Tory party; and even to-day are not able , to see eye to eye with that party upon many subjects that have to be suspended in order to gratify' Mr. Parnell through ; the agency of Mr. Gladstone. Your correspondent should first of all consider the motives that have been the means of compelling geod r Radicals to adopt their present course of action, and the causes which have directly led to it., ixt the first place, we 4 - cannot accept Mr. Gladstone's Measure because we cannot find adequate sectri.y in the safeguards embodied in it, and hence in the end it must lead to separation ,between Ireland ; and Great B•i'ain. " Unionist " mist not forget that . since the rejection of Mr. Gladstone's scheme, Mr. , Chamberlain and bir 0. Trevelysm have shown their

acceptance of Home Rule by endeavouring to come to some agreement with the Liberal leader. Sir William Harcourt, who represented Mr. Gladstone at the Round Table Confer- ence, summed it up by saying rccently that they were agreed, on the main points, and that the points on which they differed were few and secondary, and yet, strange to say, the negotiations have fallen through. Well now, does this not really show on the face of it that Mr. Gladstone adheres to his original plan, and will neither propose modi- fications to the bill which was dead, but which seems to have, at the first available oppportunity, a resurrection? We often hear about Mr. Gladstone having been willing to accept certain changes before the second reading of his Irish Government Bill, but they were so vague that in the minds of those who sought to obtain definite pledges they I committed him to nothing, and this caused the bill to be lost. Exactly the same thing has occurred at the Round Table Conference. Mr. Chamberlain has stated his objec- tions in an upright and straightforward manner, and what concessions he and his friends were prepared to make. This is just as it should be, to go into arbitration with openness and candour. According to Sir William Harcourt the whole ground was gene over, and a working agreement, that was to bring about re-union of the Liberal party, and also a united party in support of a workable plan of Home Rule might have been arrived at. Mr. Chamberlain truly said that there was a hitch somewhere, and that there was one man, viz., Mt. Gladstone, who could in a few frank sentences, settle the dispute. Mr. Gladstone is still unmoved, and evidently intends to be, in spite of his former statements that he is willing to consider reasonable changes, in order to make his scheme a workable one and secure the integrity of the Empire. I want your correspondent to ask himself what choice the Liberals have, who are compelled to dissent from Mr. Gladstone's scheme, but to support- the present Govern- ment? If they assist Mr. Gladstone to return ta power, they will help him to come back with the intention of re- newing his mistaken scheme, which they believe to be dangerous to the peace and prosperity of Ireland, nay, even the safety of the United Kingdom. With regard to coercion. the Liberal Unionists would cer- tainly demand that remedial legislation should go hand in hand together. But whether or net, when the Government of the country declares that, without further powers, it is impossible to maintain law and order in parts of Ireland, then I contend it is the bounden duty of the legitimate Opposition to sink all party differences, and render to the Government every help in their power in order to enable the Government to protect those who are unable to resist the tyranny and oppression of the National League. It is all very well for " Unionist " to write as he does, when be is safe from this anarchical combination, because he lives in this much despised country in the eyes of the Irish. Here he is at liberty to bey and sell, but in Ireland he would have the choice of being prevented from doing either it he refused to ally himself with the evil doings of the National League.—l remain, yours respectfully, A REAL UNIONIST.

div.head: MONARCHICAL DELUSION.
div.p: THE MONARCHICAL DELUSION.

find that in the minds of many people there is a fancy for maintaining what is at the same time acknow- ledged to be a delusion. F seems to spring from a distaste to change, or a feeling of opposition to anything that calls for a little exertion in the way of political thought. Looking into some matters pertaining to what is now engaging almost the whole of Englishmen's attention, Yix., the worship of a monarch, it seems that we Europeans pay to our Queens, Emperors, and Kaisers yearly not less than £5,000,000. It struck me that we were like Old Hamphray's boy—paying too dear for our whistle. As a mere theoreti- cal question I should not object to this, because' since the death of Albert the Good, we have had it proved to us over and over again, that the monarch need not necessarily be one of real flesh and blood; but, if need be, could bi substituted by a gilt throne and an ermined cloak. We have, yearly, Parliament opened and the Queen's Speech read by deputy. We have seen that British interests go on quite as well without the presence of her Majesty and her beloved heir, as during their presence. In fact, were it not for the ancient fiction that the sovereign forms one of the three estates of the realm, her Majesty might take the whole of her brood to Balmoral, and there end her days in peace and quietness, satisfied that her loyal subjects were doing as well without her as ever they did with her.

It may be that there are amongst your readers some who may object to this kind of writing, and denounce it as childish, and, at least, as derogatory to Her Majesty. Well, I have no wish to speak harshly of the Queen; she is ti:e first of the Hanoverian line that has had the good sense to " let well alone," although those who have read the late Baron Steckmar's memoirs know how near Albert the Good led her to trouble, and to the possible downfall of her most ex- pensive dynasty. To realise fully the questionable blessings of Royalty it is necessary to go a long way back. It is, in fact, necessary to absolve Her Majesty of all the sins, high crimes, and misdemeanours' of her reign. I prefer doing that, as it takes all the personal venom out of one's pen, and makes it a general question. I thiak there is no subject so full of in- terest as the one cennecte I with our Funding system. In its details we have the secret history of Royalty, and the rascality of our aristocracy. By its help taxation without representation can be carried on, and only those who profit by it are aware how the helpless poor are fleeced. In 1688 the aristocratical robbers awoke to the knowledge that their position was unsafe. Having eight years previous got rid of their feudal obligations, they saw how desirable it was to have somethine more than a mere Act of Parliament to enable them to convert the nation's land into private property. So in 1688 they des. troyed the supremacy of the crown, and got rid of the old castona of paying members for their services. They got rid of annual parliaments, and passed the Triennial Act, and in 1716 they abolished the Triennial Act and passed the Septennial Act. So England was converted into an Oligarchy, or government by a small number of aristocratic families. I think it is hardly necessary to point out that an Act of Parliament will not be necessary to put an end to the oligarchical or monarchical systems; we are growing out of them. Having destroyed the so-called constitution of the country, the aristocrats resolved to tax the people at pleasure, without the people being at all represented. The country from this period was constantly at war. The nobles, in their wild career of plunder, determined to pledge the labour of unborn generations, and so commenced what we now know as the Funding System, a system that has had many apt illustrations in our own day, notably so in the eagerness with which the Tories have rushed into war, not caring how or when their bills were maid. I may give two illustrations, out of a many, of the way in which money was borrowed. The war of 1688 cost £32,010,000; there was raised in taxation £l2 000,000, in loans £20,000,000, and, taking the interest at only 31 per cent, up to 1880 the interest amounted to £135,000,000 for the supposed loan of £20,000,000. The war of the Spanish succession, a question in which we had no interest, cost £62,500,000, of which £32,500 was raised ae loans, the interest on which, at 31 per cent, has cost us £184,625,000. To pay the interest on the national debt, which is chiefly a war debt, ninepence of every shil- ling we pay in taxes is swallowed up. Respect for pro- perty seems to me to be all on one side ; no one seems to have any respect for the rights of labour. It is a very easy matter tor readers to be misled when reading of the national debt, in this way. In 1688 occured the Whig revolution. During this reign we borrowed £41,100,795, but of this only £31.034,518, was received by Government. There was a difference here to the fund- holders benefit of £7,066,277. But the £41,100,795 was entered to the credit of the parties and interest paid on that amount, and the country was defrauded out of the £7,066,277. This is how our national debt has been built up; and it is this system of 1 organised robbery that we workmen are asked to respect to- day. In a Report issued by the House of Commons in 1816 it was distinctly shown that for every £6O borrowed by the Government £lOO was put down. Talk of national faith , and national honour, we see it in its reselts, when we take up some able report such as the one issued by Mr. Leone Levi in 1879 in which he tells us that the charge on labour yearly is £30,000.000 or a third of the sum paid in wages, that is £90,000,000. I have before me a list of the wars since 1688, with their cost. I should not like to saddle them on Her Majesty. All the same, each war had had the blessings, and, prayers of the Church, for the parsons never tire of telling us that the "Lord is 3 mighty man of war." Dating from 1833 we I have had twelve ware en hand, at a Cost of £102,116,727. Her Majesty's reign has certainly been a glorious one; no thanks to her. What has it been during the last 12 years? and what will it be in the coming years These are questions well deserving the serious attention of all. We encourage everything of a warlike tendency, and the man is called a coward who raises his voice against it; we forget the amount of moral courage required to put forth plain truths.

A return has just been issued showing what we spend on warlike inventions. I never saw what we spent on peace inveations. In 1878 we paid £5O to Mr. Armstrong for patent gun carriages. In 1880 Mr. Fraser received £5.000 for "plan of making carriages." Mr. Richards received .£3OO for "cartridges for gatling grans," and so on through a hundred names, one man, Mr. Nordenfeldt, receiving £lO,OOO for "patent ammunition," and as a fitting climax Mrs. Padwick received £lOO for "suggestion by her late husband respecting studded projectiles" I have no hesita- tion in saying that the present monarchical, aristocratical, and clerical syetem under which we are living is one well calcul ited to bring England toppling over to her ruin. Bribery seems to be at the root of all our public business revelations of a sensational kiod are every day made in the newspaper& It may be said this has nothing to do with Royalty. I answer the institution is supported because it affOrds. facilities for corruption. Take the house of Roths- childs, which contracted under a Tory Government a loan by which it made 20 per cent.; at the following election it voted Tory. In conclusion, allow toe to point out to those who have so great a respect for the national honour that, at the close or the French war in 1816, a Select Committee of the Rouse of Commons reported with regard to the Three Per Cent. Stock of .4580,016,010. that only £348,519,612 had actually been lent. To pay interest on these transactions is what we workmen labour for.

div.head: TBE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 9, 18871
div.p: TBE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 9, 18871

• THE MANCHESTER- SHIPIOANAL. ' At the ordinary quarterly meeting of the Rams- , ,bott3m Industrial and Provident Society, held on I Saturday, it was resolved to take up 50 .£lO shares in the Manchester Ship Cfnal Company. On Monday evening a well-attended meeting of residents in Leigh was held at the Courts Hotel to promote the interests of the Manchester Ship Canal. ' The meeting was presided over by Mr. John Green, Lowton, and he expressed his confidence in the scheme, believing in the directorate, and that a good dividend would accrue from the canal. Mr. Rayner, Ibarrister, and Mr. J. H. Hill, Manchester, in spirited addresses, advocated the scheme. Sevisral shares were taken at the close. On Monday night, a a meeting of the Cobden Working-men's Liberal-Club, Bury, a resolution was passed wishing every succes to the Ship Canal,l pledging the meeting to take up shares, and ex- pressing a hope that other clubs would act in a similar way. A committee was appointed to carry out the resolution, and over £l,OOO worth of shares were taken up. Alderman Crossland presided, and great enthusiasm was manifested. An influential meeting, convened by the Mayor, was held on Monday night in the Town Hall; Oldham, to further the Ship Canal scheme. Messrs. Platt, Moseley, and Bythell, directors of the Canal Company, were present, epd addressed the meet- ing. It was announced at the close that new shares to the amount of over £40,000 had been taken up in the room. • A large meeting of shareholders in the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company and others interested in the project was held on Tuesday evening in St. James's Hall, Manchester. ' Several thousand persons were present. Sir Joseph C. Lee, vice-chairman of the board of directors, presided. He said that applica- tions had been received for shares to the value of .£1" 650 000. He believed the shareholders would in every possible way assist the board to raise the remainder of the sum Whieh it is necessary should be subscribed in Manchester and district before the 1£5,000,000 is made up by London capitalists. They had only a short time before them .in which to do so, but it would be easily done if every man would do his duty. Other addresses were delivered by Idirectors, who spoke hopefully of the money being i forthcoming, and with thorough confidence n the success of the Canal as a commercial investment. In the afternoon a deputation of directors at- tended the Manchester Stock Exchange, and re- ceived promises of support from the members pre- sent.

Garnett; W. Hodgkirusin, Jahn ,Palrel6ugh, n. J. Longton, C. Jackson, Holmes, If. E. Lees, a Leigh, John Hutchings; W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), and Marshal' Stevens (general manager of the canal company.)—The MAYOR said that he had received a letter from Mr. Ziba Arinitage who wrote that he .regretted he could not be at the meeting owing -to a previous engagement. His brother was also out of town. They had both strong hopes that the scheme would go forward, and he might mention that their firm (Messrs. Armitage and Rigby) made ap- plication the previous week for 200 shares, and fur- ther that his brother (Mr. S. It, Armitage) intended to apply.for 500 shares. (Applause.)—On the motion of `Aldermanßunonss, the Mayor was elected chair- man of the committee, Mr. J. L. Tunstall being appointed secretary.—The Mason remarked that he - hoped the people of the town would take the matter up, and sustain the scheme as far as they possibly could. (Hear, hear.)—A discussion next took place as to the best way of canvassing the town to induce people to take ,up shares, • and it was ultimaely resolved to forma small committee for each of the polling districts of We town. All those present volunteered to serve on one or other of the com- mittees. It was also mentioned by Mr. Marshall Stevens thatit was the intention of Mr. Leader , Williams to bring to Warrington the model of the ' Ship Canal in about a fortnight,and give an explana- tion of it.—On the motion of Mr. Tusgraix, a local executive- committee was appointed, consisting of the Mayor; Alderman Burgess, Messrs. Monks, Geddes; Hutchings, Dakin, J. Pierpoint, T. Jolley, D. Garnett, J. rairclough, R. A. Naylor, and W. Long. —The MAYOit suggested that it would bean induce- ment to take Up shares if those present would show their confidence in the scheme by putting their names down for a certain number.—The sheet was then sent round, and it was announced that no fewer than 1,655 shares, of the value of £16,550, had been taken up that night, although many of the gentlemen present had previously taken up other shares. The meeting was then brought to a close, it being understood that canvassing would commence to-day (Saturday) in some of the districts.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
It is stated that Mr. Gladstone will make an important speech at the next house dinner of the Eighty Club on the 19th inst.

The weather being beautifully fine, the Crystal Palace and other places of amusement in London were largely pa- tronised on Good Friday. The trial receipts of 33 of the principal railways of the United Kingdom in the three months of 1887 just closed show an increase over the corresponding period of 1886 of no less than £401,085. THE UNDER SEIRETART FOR IRELAND.—The Central INews is authoritatively informed that Colonel King Har- man, M.P., has been appointed Under Secretary for Ireland. As a resident landlord, that honourable and gallant gentle- man is intimately acquainted with Ireland and Irish affairs. lie is lieutenant and custes rotulorum of County Roscom- mon, and a magistrate in three other counties. SETTLEMENT OF THE ASHTON STRIKE. The strike Which has been carried on for about four months by the Ashton weavers, who sought to obtain for specified classes of goods the rate of wages paid in other Lancashire towns, has terminated. At a conference held to discuss the matter in dispute, the employers have agreed to pay the "Nelson list" for all goods to which it applies, and arrangements I were entered iota for paying jacquard weavers. The opera- tives will resume work on Monday. ITHE OUTBREAK OF ANTHRAIL—The " Gazette" of Friday evening publishes a table showing the nualher of places in Great Britain upon which anthrax has been reported to have ! existed. During the week, ended April 2nd, three fresh I, outbreaks occurred; and total number reported upon during the week was six. Three animals remained diseased. For ! the week ended the 2nd inst., of the diseased animate five were killed, twelve died, and three remained under treat- merit. Three fresh outbreaks occurred in Essex, Notts, and the West Riding of Yorkshire. ' THE CREWE MURDER.—The young man Bevin, who is ' charged With murdering his aunt, Mrs. Griffiths, at Crewe, ' and with attempting to murder his cousin, Mary Jones, nine years old, was on Thursday evening confronted with the girl, who had recovered sufficiently to be able to give evi- dence. She deposed to going out on an errand, leaving Bevin and Mrs. Griffiths in the house. On her return she was met by the prisoner, who knocked her down and beat her in the most violent manner about the head. It was dur- leg the girl's absence that Mrs. Griffiths was murdered. . Bevin, who made no reply to this direct acpusatien, was ! further remanded.

THE QUEEN ON THE CONTINENT. Aix LP.s.BAINB, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The Queen drove out this morning. She was much disappointed at not being able to attend divine service, owing to the non-arrival of the British chaplain.
[then
MARKETS.

Mr. Nemon next gave an address, after which Miss Mice Fairhurst rendered a song in excellent style. A recitation was also given by Mr. Josemh Ellison, and another anthem by the choir. f The Rev. E. 310011 E next gave an address, at the outset of which ho joined with the chairman in ex- pressing the desirability of Christian union. There was, he continued, great need at the present time to be very faithful to the great charge Christ had comniitted to them. He believed the times were critical. Wherever they looked there -were matters that should fill them with anxiety, "though, of course, they had no doubt as to the ultimate issue. i Even n our national affairs there was much to cause them anxiety. Our drink bill again is ter- rific, and though fess than last year, it is a frightful thing still. Then there Was the fearful war spirit abroad, which might work great evil to the world. There was another thing he would mention at the risk of being.misrepresented. There were, as many ef them believed, mischievous things going on in their own land and in our own Parliament. Efforts were being made to still further increase the bon- dage, the oppression, and restrictions of the liberty tinder which 'a whole nation had groaned many score k of years. Re would say, with- out hesitation, that the policy which is being prtfßueel at the present moment by those in authority in this country had a most mischievous effect upon the religion of this country, and for the reason that whatever affected our national interests inevitably affected our national religion 4 The more they alienated men from a great Protestant country, and the more they drove them into sympathy and close relationship with the Roman Catholic hier- archy, the more they hindered the spread of truth and the simple faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. From this standpoint he viewed with the utmost con- sternation and indignition the effort now being made to forge fetters for our brethren in Ireland, and to bring them beneath the heel of a despotism

div.head: MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

On Wednesday afternoon a meeting, convened by circular by the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, Warring- ton, in furtherance of the Ship Canal scheme. The Mayor presided, and there was a good attendance of local manufacturers and others, including Messrs Bythell, Crossley, and IL Boddington, of Manches- ter, directors of the Ship Canal Company. The MAYOR said they had met together to con- sider what was the best way they in Warrington could aid the Ship Canal scheme. He, and he thought almost everyone else in Warrington thcught the canal if made would be a good thing for the town. Individually, he could not say that he had any interest in it with the exception of having to sell some land to the promoters. At the commence- ment of the project he supported it by a subscrip- tion, and since then he had given some further aid; and he had always maintained that the canal would be a good thing, not only for Manchester, but for Warrington also. (Hear, hear.) He thought that in time the Government of this country would see the advisability of taking in hand the promotioa of such,great schemes as that for the 'benefit of the community as a whole, but what they had to do that day was to see what they could do in Warring- ton towards the raising of funds sufficient to enable the promoters to make a start with the canal. He moved "That this meeting hereby pledges itself to ,do all that lies in its power to help forward the successful' floating of the Manchester Ship Canal, and that the representatives of the various branches of trade, here assembled, pledge themselves to prc- mote the scheme by taking up shares themselves, and by inducing as far as possible, others to take up shares in their respective branches. Mr. R. A. NAYLOR seconded this proposal. As a manufacturer in the town, he said, he was taking up a number of shares in the canal, and the previous night their workmen met, and he understood that they would be ready to take up amongst them as many shares as he was prepared to do himself. (Applause.) Referring to the high rates in War- rington, he said that if the Syip Canal were made the town would increase in Sin, and instead of having to pay 30 per tent on the assessment the payment would be spread over a larger area, and-probably reduced to something like. 20 per cent. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. LONG asked if, in the ease Of a working- man having a .ZlO share in the canal, it could be transferred to his family at his death without a costly legal process. Mr. E. J. Nrcnorsorr replied that in case of the man holding a £lO share dying intestate, it could be transferred to his widow through the County Court for ft few shillings. Mr. HUTCHINGS spoke in favour of the canal scheme, and explained the method that was adopted to enable his workmen to take up shares. Mr. H. Wrirrnem said that working-men had been often referred to at that meeting, but he did not think there were two representative working- men present. He thought the time of day at which the meeting was held was not oppor- tune for working-men. (Hear, hear.) With respect to working-men subscribing their sav- ings to that scheme, he must say the em- ployers in the town had not come forward in a sufficiently straightforward,faahion to support tAie scheme, and workmen thought it would be foolish- ness on their part to risk their money when their employers did not risk theirs. (Hear, hear.) In fact be knew that some employers in the town had advised their workmen not to subscribe to the scheme. He had also been sorry to seethe Corpora- tion so lukewarm in the scheme. . .

_ Mr. F. Moisics suggested that those present at that meeting should form themselves into a com- mittee to promote the scheme. The canal, he be- lieve, would be of such immense benefit to War- rington that it was every man's duty to do his best to further it. (Hear, hear.) He also suggested that the directors present 'night give them an idea of what they considered would be a fair quota from! Warringion in aid of the scheme. Mr. CROSSLEY and Mr. BYTHELL (directors) next addressed the meeting in advocacy of the Canal Scheme, and in answer ,to Mr. Monk's question, the latter gentleman said that he thought that sub- scriptions of £1.50,000 to £250,000 should not be ex- cessive for Warrington. Mr. GEO. WOODS, Mr. LEADER WILLIAMS (en- gineer of the scheme), Mr. H. BonnixeroN (direc- tor), next addressed the meeting. Letters were also read from Mr. James Nicholson, Thelwall Hall, and MT. R. Davies, Warrington. The former gentle- man said he had sent in a substantial application for shares; and Mr. Davies wrote that he would take .£l.OO worth of shares for each of his three sons. (Applause.) Mr. T. JOLLEY supported Mr. Monk's suggestion that a committee be formed.
The resolution proposed by the Mayor was then carried. _ _ _

Alderman BIIROBSS next moved "That the gen- tlemen present do hereby resolve themselves into a committee with power to add to their number to give effect to the resolution just rpassed." (Ap- plause.) Mr. F. MONKS seconded this proposal. Referring to the advantages that would be conferred by the canal, he said that in the case of their own firm their present rate was 15s. per ton to Glasgow, but he did not hesitate to say that if they had the canal they could bring goods from Glasgow along- side their works at 4s. per ton. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. LONG supported the resolution. He mentioned that at first he had been sceptical as to the merits of the scheme, but he was now convinced that it would be a success. He had made applica- tion for some shares and he was ready to take more if the people of the town came forward as he ex- pected they wOuld. (Hear, hear.) He did hope that Warrington would show herself in her true colours in regard to this matter and give a hearty support to the scheme. If she did not, she would re- gret it as long as she was Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then carried unanimously. It was also agreed that a further meeting should be held the next evening. A vote of thanks to the Mayor, on the motion of Mr. CROSSLEY, seconded by Mr. BODDINGTON. brought the proceed inns to a close. ADJOURNED MEETING: NUMEROUS SHARES

TAKEN UP. The adjourned meeting of the committee was held on Thursday evening in the Council Chamber, Town Hall. The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Presided, and amongst others present were Alderman Bur- gess; Councillors T. Jolley, G. Dakin, and J. Pier- point; Messrs. F. Monks, J. L Tunstall„T. Tunstall. J. div.head: MERSEY MYSTERY. A. WIDNES BQY MISSING.
div.p: A MERSEY MYSTERY. A. WIDNES BQY MISSING.

No tidings lave yet been received of the boy ElHerm, who•-jumped into the Arersey, at Liverpool, from the training ship Indefatigable a few days ago with the object of snaking his escape. On Saturday two of the lads, of whom Ellison wag one, whilst their shipmates were at prayers undressed themselves, and slinging their clothes in a bundle over their backs, jumped Into the river. As an explanation of Elli- son's conduct; it is said that ho previously expressed a desire to get ashore and go to his home in Widnes, but that permission was refused. Those on board the vessel made a seisroh for the missing boys, and found Parry below, he having citing to the chain cable and climbed into the ship. Ellison was never seen Afterwards. On Sunday the nude body of a boy about sixteen years of age was picked up in the river off the Waterloo Dock, awl conveyed to the mortuary at the Prince's Dock, where it still remains. This body was considered to be that of the missing boy, and the opinion was strengthened when, on Monday morning, an officer of the ship and several boys viewed it, and, we are in- formed, expressed their decided belief that it was that of Eason.• Strange to say, however, this statement was withdrawn, and at the inquest, which took place on Tuesday, no one from the Indefatigable was call( d to give evidence. It was, of course, impossible for the eity coroner to call a witness who could not say Whether the body was that of Ellison or not. Such evidence would be of no valise, and the jury, under the circumstances, could do- nothing but return the verdict of • Found drowned" in accordance with the evidence of Dr.Lowndes,islo made the postmortem examination. The distressed widowed mother of the boy Ellison, who was said to be a good swimmer, went to Liver- pool on Tuesday, from Widnes, and in the afternoon visited the training ship. She did not, however, view the body at the deadhonse. The superinten- dent's (Copt* John Oroome's) official report of the occurrence submitted to the committee of the ship is as follows ;—" On Saturday evening, at 8 15, when the boys were mustering for prayers, found John

Ellison and Albery Parry were rbst,nt. Search was made for them, and Parry was found naked in .he washhouse. It appears they had made it up to swim on shore, but Parry, not being able to swim, had worked his way up the gangway. Ellison, being a good swimmer. escaped. A boat was lowered and search was made, but could not find any trace of him."

THE EPIDEMIC OF MEASLES. The" British Medical Journal" Bays: "Measles has been more or lees prevalent at Warrington since September: 1886, when it appeared thitt the cafes were asociated specially with one infants' school, which was closed during the months of October and November, and then came a cessation, but more cases were notified in December. In the month of January the number of notifications was 104, and there were 8 deaths; in February, 141 and 16 deaths; and in, March, 371 and 33 deaths, giving a total of 614 cases in the same number of dwellings. and 57 depths. Dr. Gornall, the medical officer of health, is of opinion that the epidemic has been principally promoted by the children attending school in the early stage of Mid disease, and return- ing to school before they ceased to be infective, and by the gross carelessness of parents visiting, with children in their arms, houses wherethe disease ex- isted, and allowing children to go into infected houses. Amongst the difficulties which medical officers have to contend with in coping- with an outbreak of measles is the tendency of teachers to Induce parents to send their children back to school before the infective stage hits passed. Dr. Gornall points out—and this is a very, important matter which requires further investigation—that though the Educational Department of the Local Govern- ment Board assures the teachers that absence from school on account of epidemic diseases will be allowed for in estimating the grant, teachers are loud in their complaints that when the examina- tions are held this is lost sight of. Several of the schools have been closed, and everything which medical science and sanitation can suggest has been doneby the medical officer of health and his staff to stay the epidemic."

div.head: MISSIONARY 'MEETING:
div.p: MISSIONARY 'MEETING:

Yesterday the Wesleyan missionary anniversary was celebrated at Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, Warrington. In the morning the Rev. R. W. Starr, of Bolton, preached an excellent sermon to a large congregation, and in the evening the annual mis- sionary meeting was held in the chapel. There was a good congregation. The chair was occupied by Mr. Wiliam Bennett, and amongst those also present were the Revs. R. W. Starr, W. Wilson (deputation), G. E. Young (superintendent of the Warrington Circuit), J. 11. Jones, G. E. Cutting, Mr. E. J. Guest, Mr. Wright, &c.—Hymns having been sung and prayer offered up by the Rev. J. H. Jones, the CHAIRMAN called upon Mr. Wright to read the financial report.—Mr. WRIGHT prefaced the report lby remarking that there had been an increase in the income of the Missionary Society, for that cir- cuit, of £2l this year. (Applause.) Warrington itself (Bold-street and Bensey-road) had con- tributed a total of £lO5 13s, an increase of £l4. Moore contributed £23 9s, Padgate £2O. Pdnketh ..£l9 14s Bd, Lymm £l2 3s 6d, Appleton £lO 108 2d, Sankey Bridges £B, Latchford £7 118 4d, Antrobus .£7 10s, Whitley £6 19s Id, Hatton £4 28, Martins- croft £1 2s 6d, making a full total of £225 odd. He trusted that the income of , the circuit *Mild go on increasing, and then proposed committee for the ensuing year. The Rev. G. E. CUTTING seconded the proposition, and proceeded to read the general report, which was of an interesting nature. The ekperience of another year, it was remarked, had given the society me misgiving as to the final success of the work, and the desire for a general advance expressed at the last conference had been realised. The work was progressing in France. Brussels, and Germany. Austria continued to be the only country in the world where Methodists were not allowed the right of free public worship. In Spain the year had been one of trial, and in Portugal the work was still limited to theneighbourhood of Oporto. The struggle with financial difficulties continued in northern Italy, but the work of evangelisation was steadily carried on as far as funds would permit. The work was prospering in Ceylon, • India, find China. The report concluded by stating that the demands of the year had exceeded the resources, and monetary aid was much wanted.—The CHAIR- MAN then gave a short address, in the course of which he remarked that when it was considered how many people in foreign parts were perishing for lack of religious knowledge, it would be seen that their efforts to help on the good cause must not be reiaxen. It, was no mean sacrifice that was made by those who went out to be missionaries in foreign lands, and all praise was due to theni They should all do their beat to help on this noble work, and, as this was the jubilee year of the Queen's reign, it would ,be ir good thing if a special effort were made in aid of the missions. (Applause.)— Other addresses were afterwards given, and collec- tions were made in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions.

div.head: FOOTBALL MATCHES.
div.p: FOOTBALL MATCHES.

Football is to hold a prominent place in connec- tion with the Easter holidays in Warrington this year. Yesterday the premier local team journeyed to Oldham, to-day they. will visit Bradford to play tile well-known Manmngham team; on Monday Oldham will pay their return visit to Warrington; and on Tuesday admirers of football in this locality will have the pleasure of witnessing an encounter between the local team and the famous Wakefield Trinity, who now hold the torkshire Cup for the fourth time. The bringing off of this last-named fix- ture is looked forward to with much interest, and a splendid game is sure to be witnessed, as the local •men will doubtless strain every nerve in order to show .well in comparison with „their redoubtable opponents. It should be mentioned that in addi- tion to first team matches, Warrington "A " team yesterday met and defeated Oldham "A" team, and to-day meet the "A " of Widnes Recreation Club: WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM (" A " TEAMS).

Yesterday a match was played between these two teams on the Warrington ground, in the presence of A very large gathering of spectators. The ball was set in motion by Boardman, on behalf of Warrington' and that player follow- ing up, held the full back with the ball. A few moments' play, and Oldham were forced to concede a touch down. On the kick out the leather was again promptly carried towards the visitors, the result being another minor point to the credit of the home team. Some scrimmages in pretty close proximity to the visitors' line were the next feature of the game. By some smart play, however, they managed to relieve to centre, lint the ball was soon brought bick by Appletoo, who made a splendid ran, and was just brought down when a yard or two from the line. .Shortly after Ap- pleton repeated this feat, but the visitors again managed to relieve their lines. Getting the bell from a scrimmage in centre, Unsworth put in a tine run, but Oldham managed to save. At this point Appleton retired, having hurt hie ahoulder. Play, however, continued in the visitors' half, and a third touchdown was conceded to the home team, and this was followed by a fourth and fifth, after the ball had travelled about rather rapidly for some time. In the second half Warrington continued to assert their superiority, and a prominent feature of this part was a powerful run by Hackett. Nevins and Boaidman likewise showed up well. Oldham now began to press their opponents 3omewbat, and in the end Jolley was compelled to touch down. This advantage was, however, quickly counteracted, for the Oldham quarters again became the scene of hostilities. and as the result of some really good passing amongst the Warrington forwards Randalls suc- ceeded in grounding a try in a good position. Boardman, however, failed at the place. Later on Randalls by a clever run again managed to get over, but Boardman again failed to secure the major point. After a fast game War- rington won by two tries and •six minors to Oldham one minor. The Warrington team, who all played well, were— Full back, Jolley; three.quarter backs, Boardman, Apple- ton, Belshaw ; half-backs, Hackett and Jones; forwards, Ashurstt, Molyneux, Bate, Thornley, Unsworth, Eyes, Ran- dalls, Nevins, and Coyne. Referee, Mr. Tatham, Widnes. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM.

The Warrington team met Oldham yesterday, on the ground of the latter club, in beautiful weather. There were about 2,000 spectators oil the field. The kick off was at six o'clock, two " thirties" being played. Warrington during the first half had much the best of the game, but were un- lucky in scoring only a try, this being by Fair Turner be- tween the posts, Bpeakman failing at goal. Clough got a try for the home team, from which Rhodes kicked a goal, and at the call of time the game resulted in a win for the Oldham team, the score being : Oldham, one goal and two minors, to Warrington, one try and three minors. Teims : Warrington—Full back, Frank Turner; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Massey, and W Lund ; half backs, Speakman and Antrobus ; forwards, Ashton (captain), Fair Turner, Rigby, Povev, Davies Cragan, Littlewood, Adamson, and Hayes. Oldbant—Fall back, J T Walkden ; three-quarter backs, Greaves, Mills, and"Clough ; half-backs, Holden and 11 Wolstencroft ; forwards, ffalkyard, Ripley, Thwaite, T Taylor, James Taylor, E Wood, Whitehead, J Wolstencreft, and Rhodes.
